prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Have you ever bought something expensive and then found yourself reading lots of good reviews about it, after you'd already bought it? That's a clue to today's topic: cognitive dissonance. The term comes from the psychologist Leon Festinger in the 1950s. Dissonance is the uncomfortable tension we feel when we hold two ideas that don't fit together, or when our actions don't match our beliefs. And because it's uncomfortable, we're motivated to reduce it, often by changing a belief. The classic experiment was published in 1959. Students spent an hour doing extremely boring tasks, like turning wooden pegs a quarter turn, again and again. Then they were asked to tell the next participant that the task was fun and interesting. Some were paid one dollar for telling this lie, and others were paid twenty dollars. Afterward, everyone rated how enjoyable the task really was. So, who do you think rated it higher? Most people guess the twenty-dollar group. But it was the one-dollar group. Why? The twenty-dollar students had a good reason for lying: the money. Little dissonance. The one-dollar students didn't. One dollar isn't much of a reason to lie. So, to make sense of what they'd done, they shifted their belief: maybe the task wasn't so bad after all. That's the opposite of what a simple reward theory would predict. More reward produced less change in attitude.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: If you hide a toy under a blanket in front of a six-month-old baby, the baby usually won't search for it. It's as if the toy has stopped existing. The Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget saw this as evidence that young infants lack object permanence, the understanding that things continue to exist when we can't see them. In his view, it isn't firmly in place until around the end of the first year. Now, notice what Piaget's test requires. To pass it, the baby has to plan an action: reach out, lift the blanket, grab the toy. What if babies understand more than they can show with their hands? Starting in the 1980s, researchers used a different method, called violation of expectation. The idea is simple: babies look longer at events that surprise them. In one well-known study, babies watched a screen rotate back toward a box that should have stopped it. In the impossible version, the screen seemed to pass right through the box. Babies as young as four or five months looked longer at the impossible event, which suggests they expected the hidden box to still be there. But here's the debate. Critics argue that longer looking doesn't necessarily mean surprise based on understanding. Babies might simply be reacting to something new. So the question becomes: how much can we read into a baby's gaze?

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Today we're looking at one of the most widely used procedures in developmental psychology. It's called the Strange Situation, and it was designed by Mary Ainsworth in the 1970s to study attachment, the emotional bond between an infant and a caregiver. So, how does it work? A parent and a baby, usually about a year old, come into an unfamiliar room with toys. Over about twenty minutes, a series of short episodes takes place. A stranger enters. The parent leaves the baby with the stranger for a few minutes, then returns. Later the baby is left completely alone, briefly. Now, you might think the key moment is when the parent leaves. But Ainsworth focused on the reunion, what the baby does when the parent comes back. Securely attached babies may cry when the parent leaves, but when the parent returns, they seek comfort, calm down fairly quickly, and go back to playing. Avoidant babies tend to ignore the parent on return, as if they didn't care. And resistant babies seek contact but also push away, staying upset and hard to soothe. Later researchers added a fourth category for behavior that seemed confused or contradictory. One caution, though. In cultures where babies are rarely separated from their mothers, or rarely left with strangers, the same procedure may be far more stressful, so the results have to be interpreted carefully.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: In 1928, the sociologist W. I. Thomas made an observation that's become a basic idea in sociology: if people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences. In other words, what people believe about a situation shapes how they act, whether or not the belief is accurate. Twenty years later, another sociologist, Robert Merton, built on this with a concept he called the self-fulfilling prophecy. That's a false belief that leads to behavior that makes the belief come true. Merton's best-known example was a bank. Imagine a bank that's perfectly healthy. It has enough assets, and it's well managed. But a rumor starts that it's about to fail. What happens? Depositors rush to take out their money, and since no bank keeps all its deposits on hand as cash, the bank really does run out. The prophecy produced the very failure it predicted. Now, Merton stressed that the original belief was false. That's what makes it self-fulfilling, rather than just an accurate prediction. Researchers have since looked for the same pattern in classrooms. A famous study in the 1960s reported that when teachers were told certain students were about to bloom academically, those students later showed greater gains. Later work, though, suggests that teacher expectations do matter, but their effects are usually smaller than that first study claimed.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: When you hear the word bureaucracy, you probably think of long lines, endless forms, and offices where nobody will help you. But for the German sociologist Max Weber, writing in the early twentieth century, bureaucracy was something more interesting. He saw it as the most efficient form of organization humans had devised. So what is a bureaucracy, in Weber's sense? It has a clear hierarchy, with each office reporting to the one above. Tasks are divided among specialists. Decisions follow written rules and are recorded in files. And officials are hired for their qualifications, not because they're someone's relative or friend. Notice that last point. Compared with older systems, where positions were handed out through personal loyalty, bureaucracy was in a sense fairer. Everyone is treated by the same rules, impersonally. That predictability is what made it so powerful. Yet Weber was deeply uneasy about it. As rational rules spread through government, business, and everyday life, he feared that people would become trapped in systems they couldn't escape, valued only for their function. His image for this is usually translated into English as the iron cage. Actually, the German phrase is closer to 'a shell as hard as steel,' which suggests something we come to wear, not just something around us. So Weber's view was neither simply for nor against bureaucracy. Its strengths and dangers came from the same source.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: In 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay called 'The Tragedy of the Commons,' and it became one of the most cited arguments in the social sciences. Here's his scenario. Imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each herder thinks: if I add one more cow, I get all the benefit of that cow, but the cost, a little less grass, is shared by everyone. So it's rational for each herder to add another cow, and another. The result, Hardin argued, is that the pasture is overgrazed and ruined. Individual rationality leads to collective disaster. His solutions were essentially two: divide the land into private property, or have the government regulate its use. Now, the political economist Elinor Ostrom challenged this. She studied real communities that had managed shared resources for generations: alpine meadows in Switzerland, forests in Japan, irrigation systems in Spain. These weren't free-for-alls. prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Okay, here's a puzzle. Suppose one country can produce everything more efficiently than another country. Should it bother to trade with that country at all? It seems like the answer should be no. But in 1817, the economist David Ricardo showed why the answer is actually yes. His example used England and Portugal, and two goods, cloth and wine. In his numbers, Portugal could make both with less labor than England. Economists say Portugal had an absolute advantage in both. But Portugal's advantage was much bigger in wine than in cloth. So, Ricardo argued, Portugal should specialize in wine, England in cloth, and they should trade. Both countries end up with more of both goods. The key concept here is comparative advantage, which is about opportunity cost, what you give up to produce something. Every hour Portuguese workers spent making cloth was an hour not spent making wine, where they were especially productive. Here's an everyday version. Imagine a lawyer who types faster than her assistant. Should she do her own typing? Probably not, because every hour spent typing is an hour not spent practicing law, which earns far more. Now, the model has limits. It assumes workers can easily move from one industry to another. In reality, workers in a shrinking industry may struggle to find new jobs. So the gains are real, but they aren't shared evenly.

Why trade can benefit a country that is better at everything

explanation: The professor explains Ricardo's idea of comparative advantage and why it makes trade beneficial.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: There's an old economic principle usually summarized as 'bad money drives out good.' It's called Gresham's law, after Thomas Gresham, a sixteenth-century English financial agent, although the idea is older. What does it mean? Imagine two coins with the same official value, but one contains more silver than the other. Which one would you spend? The one with less silver, of course. You'd keep the better coin, or even melt it down, because the metal inside is worth more than the coin's face value. If everyone does this, the good coins vanish, and only the bad ones change hands. There's a well-known modern case. In 1965, the United States stopped putting silver in its dimes and quarters. Within a few years, the old silver coins had largely disappeared from everyday use, as people set them aside. Now, here's the important condition, and it's easy to miss. Gresham's law works because the law requires people to accept both coins at the same value. A shopkeeper can't say, 'I'll take your old silver quarter, but not that new one.' When that condition breaks down, the effect can reverse. During periods of very high inflation, sellers often refuse the weak local currency and demand a more stable foreign one. In that case, good money drives out bad. So whether bad money wins depends on the rules, not just on the money.

When people spend weaker money and keep better money

explanation: The professor explains Gresham's law and the condition under which it holds or reverses.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Today's topic is a man whose ideas still shape how work is organized, even if most workers have never heard of him: Frederick Winslow Taylor. In 1911, Taylor published The Principles of Scientific Management. His argument was that most work was done inefficiently, by rule of thumb, and that it could be improved through careful measurement. So, what did that look like? Taylor and his assistants used stopwatches to time each part of a job, broke tasks into their smallest motions, and searched for what he called the one best way to do them. Workers were then trained in that method, and often paid by the piece to encourage output. His most famous example involved workers loading heavy iron bars onto railroad cars. Taylor claimed that with the right method and rest breaks, one worker raised his daily load from about twelve and a half tons to forty-seven. Historians have questioned that story. But the bigger debate is about what the system did to work itself. Taylor separated the planning of work, done by managers, from the doing of it, done by workers. Supporters saw this as a major gain in productivity. Critics argued that it stripped workers of skill and judgment, turning them into parts of a machine. There were strikes against these methods, and even government hearings. Yet look at a modern warehouse. Taylor's influence is everywhere.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Why do so many prices end in ninety-nine? Two ninety-nine instead of three dollars, nineteen ninety-nine instead of twenty. One cent can't possibly matter, right? Well, research suggests it does. The practice is often called charm pricing, and one explanation for it is the left-digit effect. We read numbers from left to right, and we tend to give the first digit a lot of weight. So when we see two ninety-nine, our first impression is 'two dollars and something,' and that impression sticks, even though the price is almost exactly three dollars. The effect seems strongest when we're making quick decisions, like scanning store shelves. In one field experiment, a clothing catalog offered the same dress at different prices in different versions. Surprisingly, the dress sold more at thirty-nine dollars than at thirty-four. A price ending in nine seemed to signal a bargain. Now, you may have heard a different story about where this practice came from: that odd prices forced cashiers to open the register to make change, which made it harder to pocket the money. It's a nice story, but there's little evidence for it. And here's an exception. Sellers of luxury goods often avoid nines altogether. They use round numbers, because a price ending in nine can make a product look discounted, and that's the last thing an expensive product wants to suggest.

How luxury products are advertised to wealthy buyers

explanation: The professor explains charm pricing and the left-digit effect, along with an exception for luxury goods.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Why do some countries have two dominant political parties while others have five or six? One influential answer comes from the French political scientist Maurice Duverger. In the 1950s, he argued that election rules shape the party system. His most famous claim, now called Duverger's law, says that plurality voting in single-member districts tends to produce two-party systems. Plurality just means the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority. Duverger identified two forces. The first is mechanical: in a winner-take-all district, a party that comes third everywhere can win a decent share of the national vote but almost no seats. The second is psychological: voters anticipate this, and rather than waste their vote on a party that can't win, they shift to one of the two front-runners. By contrast, proportional representation, where seats are divided according to vote share, lets smaller parties survive, and it tends to produce many parties. Now, is it really a law? There are well-known exceptions. Some countries with plurality voting have several significant parties. The usual explanation is geography. Duverger's logic works within each district, so a party that's weak nationally but strong in one region can still win seats there, and survive. So most political scientists today treat Duverger's law less as a law than as a strong tendency, one that depends on how votes are distributed.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Think about the last time you learned something difficult, maybe a math concept or a new sport. Was there a point where you couldn't quite do it alone, but you could do it with someone guiding you? That in-between space is the heart of today's topic. The Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky, working in the 1920s and early 1930s, called it the zone of proximal development. It's the gap between what a learner can do independently and what they can do with help from someone more skilled, like a teacher or even a more experienced classmate. Now, why does that matter? Vygotsky argued that teaching is most effective when it's aimed at this zone. Too easy, and the learner doesn't grow. Too hard, and even with help, they can't succeed. Decades later, researchers introduced a related term: scaffolding. Just like the scaffolding around a building under construction, the support is temporary. A teacher might begin by breaking a task into steps, giving hints, or demonstrating. Then, as the learner gains skill, the support is gradually removed. Picture teaching a child to ride a bike. You hold the seat, then you just keep a hand near it, and eventually you let go. Notice how this differs from the view of Jean Piaget, who emphasized children discovering ideas largely on their own. For Vygotsky, learning was fundamentally social.

Teaching aimed at what learners can do with support

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Does the news change what we think? For a long time, researchers found surprisingly weak effects. People rarely changed their opinions just because of what they read or watched. But in 1963, a political scientist made an observation that redirected the field. He wrote, roughly, that the press may not be very successful at telling people what to think, but it's remarkably successful at telling them what to think about. That's the core of what we now call agenda-setting. In 1968, two researchers tested the idea in a single town in North Carolina during a presidential election. They asked undecided voters which issues they considered most important, and then measured how much coverage each issue received in the news. The match was striking. The issues that got the most coverage were the issues voters ranked as most important. Now, you should already see the problem. A match like that doesn't tell you which way the influence runs. Maybe the media simply covered what the public already cared about. So later researchers used experiments. They showed people edited newscasts that gave extra attention to one issue, and afterward, those viewers rated that issue as more important than viewers who'd seen other versions. That's much stronger evidence of cause. And the idea has grown since. Researchers now study not just which topics get attention, but which aspects of a topic are emphasized.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Look at the world map on the wall. Greenland looks about as big as Africa, doesn't it? In reality, Africa is about fourteen times larger. So what's going on? This map uses the Mercator projection, created by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator in 1569. And to understand it, you need to know what it was designed for. Mercator's goal was navigation. On his map, a line of constant compass direction appears as a straight line. So a sailor could draw a straight line from one port to another, measure the angle, and follow that compass heading. That was enormously useful. But there's a price. You can't flatten a sphere onto paper without distorting something. It's like trying to flatten an orange peel without tearing or stretching it. Mercator's map keeps angles and the shapes of small areas correct, but it stretches areas more and more as you move away from the equator. Near the poles, the stretching becomes extreme, which is why Greenland and Antarctica look enormous. Now, other projections make different trade-offs. Equal-area projections show the sizes of regions correctly, but they distort shapes, so continents can look squashed or stretched. There's no perfect flat map. Every projection is a choice about what to get right. The real problem comes when a map designed for sailors becomes the picture of the world that most people grow up with.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Why are towns spaced the way they are? Why does a small village have a bakery but not a specialist hospital? In 1933, the German geographer Walter Christaller proposed an answer, now called central place theory, based on settlements in southern Germany. The idea starts with two concepts. The first is threshold: the minimum number of customers needed to keep a business going. The second is range: the maximum distance people are willing to travel for something. Now, think about bread. People buy it often and won't travel far for it, but it doesn't take many customers to support a bakery. So bakeries appear even in small settlements. A jewelry store or a specialist doctor is the opposite. People need them rarely and will travel farther, but they need many customers. So those appear only in big cities. The result, Christaller argued, is a hierarchy: many small places offering basic goods, fewer towns offering more, and a few cities offering almost everything. He also predicted that market areas would form hexagons. Why hexagons? Because circles would either overlap or leave gaps, while hexagons fit together perfectly. prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: We often credit Johannes Gutenberg with inventing movable type around 1450. But that's not quite right. Movable type was first invented in China, in the 1040s, by a craftsman named Bi Sheng, who made individual characters out of baked clay. And in Korea, printers were using movable metal type by the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. The oldest surviving book printed with metal type is Korean, from 1377, decades before Gutenberg. So here's the question. Why did movable type transform European society so quickly, while in East Asia it remained less dominant? One major factor is the writing system. European languages use alphabets with a few dozen letters. Chinese writing uses thousands of characters. A printer working in Chinese needed an enormous stock of type, and finding and sorting each character was slow. Woodblock printing, where an entire page is carved into a single block, was often simply more practical. The blocks could be stored and reused for new print runs. So it's a mistake to see East Asia as having missed an opportunity. Printers there made a reasonable choice, and woodblock printing produced enormous numbers of books. Gutenberg's real achievement, then, wasn't the idea of movable type. It was a whole system: a mold for casting identical metal letters quickly, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a press adapted from those used to make wine.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: The Inca Empire, stretching along the Andes, ran a huge state, with roads, storehouses, and labor obligations, all without writing in the usual sense. So how did they keep records? The answer is the quipu, a set of knotted cords. A quipu has a main cord, with dozens or even hundreds of cords hanging from it. On many quipus, the knots record numbers in a base-ten system. Knots farthest from the main cord represent units, the next cluster up represents tens, then hundreds, and so on. Different types of knots made the system readable; for example, a figure-eight knot marks a one in the units position. This code was worked out in the early twentieth century, and it shows quipus were used for census counts and tribute records. The officials who made and read them were specialists. Now, here's the open question. Spanish chroniclers after the conquest reported that these specialists could recite histories, laws, and family lines from their cords. So did some quipus record language, not just numbers? A significant share of surviving quipus don't seem to fit the numerical system, and features like color, fiber, and knot direction may carry meaning. But no one has deciphered them. One problem is that the chroniclers may have misunderstood what they saw. Another is that the cords may have been memory aids, readable only by their makers.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: In the mid-1800s, most doctors in Europe believed that diseases like cholera spread through miasma, which basically means bad air, foul smells rising from rotting matter. It made sense: disease was common in crowded, smelly neighborhoods. But the London doctor John Snow suspected that cholera spread through contaminated water. In 1854, a severe outbreak struck the Soho district of London, and hundreds of people died within days. Snow went door to door, recording where the victims had lived, and he marked the deaths on a map. They clustered around a single public water pump on Broad Street. Now, some of the most persuasive evidence came from the exceptions. A nearby brewery had almost no cases. Why? The workers were given beer to drink, and the brewery had its own well, so they didn't use the pump. A nearby workhouse, also with its own well, had very few deaths. Meanwhile, a woman who lived miles away had died. It turned out she liked the taste of Broad Street water and had it brought to her house. Snow presented his findings, and local officials removed the handle of the pump. It's a famous story, but one caution: the outbreak was already declining by then, partly because many residents had fled. So removing the handle probably wasn't what ended it. The real importance was the method: careful mapping and close attention to exceptions.

How a doctor traced the source of a disease outbreak

explanation: The professor describes how John Snow linked the 1854 cholera outbreak to the Broad Street pump.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: When we talk about Impressionism, we usually talk about artists like Monet and Renoir and their interest in capturing light outdoors. But today I want to look at a humble piece of technology that helped make that possible: the paint tube. Before the 1840s, oil paint was hard to carry around. Painters, or their assistants, ground pigments by hand and mixed them with oil in the studio. If paint was stored at all, it was usually kept in small bags made from pig bladders, tied with string. You'd prick the bladder to squeeze out some paint, but the bags leaked, burst easily, and the paint dried out. Then, in 1841, an American portrait painter named John Goffe Rand patented a collapsible metal tube with a cap. Paint stayed fresh, and it could be carried anywhere. Combined with portable easels and a range of new, bright, ready-made colors, this meant painters could work outdoors, directly in front of the scene, for hours. Renoir is reported to have said that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. Now, we shouldn't overstate this. Artists had been making small oil sketches outdoors long before tubes existed. And many Impressionist paintings that look spontaneous were actually reworked or finished in the studio. So the tube didn't create the movement. But it certainly made the Impressionists' way of working far easier.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Today let's talk about an instrument you all know, whose name tells a story. Around 1700, in Florence, an instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori, who worked for the powerful Medici family, built a new kind of keyboard. Now, the dominant keyboard instrument at the time was the harpsichord. When you press a harpsichord key, a small quill plucks the string. And here's the limitation: no matter how hard or softly you press the key, the string is plucked in much the same way, so the volume barely changes. Cristofori's idea was to strike the strings with small hammers instead. The harder you press the key, the faster the hammer moves, and the louder the sound. He also solved a tricky mechanical problem: the hammer had to hit the string and then immediately fall away, so the string could keep vibrating. He called the instrument, roughly translated, a harpsichord with soft and loud, in Italian, piano e forte. And that's where our word piano comes from. Interestingly, the invention didn't catch on right away. It took decades of improvements before the piano became the instrument that composers like Mozart and Beethoven wrote for. There was one older keyboard that could vary its volume, by the way: the clavichord. But it was so quiet that it was mainly used for practice in small rooms, not for public performance.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: We tend to imagine life before farming as a constant struggle for survival, people working from dawn to dusk just to eat. In the 1960s, the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins challenged that picture with a deliberately provocative phrase: the original affluent society. His argument drew on new studies of foragers, people who live by hunting and gathering, including groups in the Kalahari Desert. Researchers had recorded how much time people actually spent getting food, and the numbers were surprisingly low, often around fifteen to twenty hours a week. So in what sense were they affluent? Sahlins pointed out that there are two ways to satisfy your wants. You can produce a lot, or you can want little. Foragers moved often, so owning many things was a burden, not a benefit. With modest wants and fairly reliable food sources, they had plenty of leisure. Now, the critique. Later anthropologists pointed out that those early figures counted only time spent hunting and gathering. They left out making tools, processing food, collecting firewood, and other household work. Include all of that, and the total comes much closer to a full working week. Studies also found seasonal hunger in some groups. So the strong version of Sahlins's claim hasn't held up. But his deeper point, that affluence depends on what people want, not only on what they have, still challenges ideas of economic progress.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: So, here's a question that sounds silly at first: who decides what time it is? Before the 1880s, the answer in the United States was basically, the sun. Each town set its clocks by local solar time, so when it was noon in Chicago, it was already a few minutes past noon in towns to the east. For a farmer, that was fine. For a railroad, it was chaos. Each company ran on its own time, and a busy station might display several clocks at once. In fact, there were dozens of separate railroad times in use. Now, Britain had faced this problem earlier, in the 1840s, and its solution was simple: the railways adopted one national time, Greenwich time. But Britain is small. The United States spans about four hours of solar time, so a single national time wouldn't work. The solution the American railroads chose was zones. On November 18, 1883, they switched to four standard time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain, and Pacific. People called it the day of two noons, because in many towns the clocks struck twelve, were set back, and later struck twelve again. A year later, in 1884, an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the world's prime meridian. But here's what surprises students. Congress didn't make the time zones official until 1918. So for thirty-five years, the time most Americans lived by was set not by the government, but by private companies. The law simply caught up.

choices.text: Why Britain chose Greenwich time for its national railways
How railroads replaced local time with a system of time zones
How Congress designed the time zones used by the railroads
Why farmers resisted giving up local solar time

sampleAnswer: How railroads replaced local time with a system of time zones
explanation: The professor explains how American railroads moved from many local times to four standard zones, long before the law required it.

prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: Today let's look at what happened to ordinary workers after the Black Death. The plague reached England in 1348, and within about two years it had killed somewhere between a third and a half of the population. Think about that economically. Suddenly there were far fewer people to plow fields and bring in harvests, but the land was still there. So laborers were scarce, and scarce things get expensive. Workers began demanding higher wages, and many simply moved to whichever lord offered the best terms. Landowners didn't like this. So the government responded in two steps. First came an emergency ordinance in 1349, and then, in 1351, the Statute of Laborers, which tried to freeze wages at their pre-plague levels and made it illegal to refuse work. Did it work? Only partly. Wages still rose, and resentment over these controls, along with new taxes, fed into the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Over the following century, serfdom in England largely faded away. Now, historians used to tell this as a simple story: the plague made labor scarce, so peasants became free. But compare England with parts of Eastern Europe, like Poland and Prussia. There, labor was also scarce compared with the amount of land, yet over the next two centuries, lords actually tightened their control, binding peasants more firmly to their estates. Same kind of shortage, opposite result. So the current view is that the plague created pressure, but what happened next depended on who held power.

How a labor shortage after the plague led to different outcomes
How the Peasants' Revolt brought the plague to an end
Why English lords offered higher wages than Polish lords

sampleAnswer: How a labor shortage after the plague led to different outcomes
explanation: The lecturer explains how the plague made labor scarce and why the results differed between England and Eastern Europe.

prompt: What is the podcast mainly about?
audioScript: Welcome back. Today's object is a lump of corroded bronze that turned out to be one of the most surprising finds in archaeology. In 1900, sponge divers sheltering from a storm near the small Greek island of Antikythera spotted a shipwreck on the seabed. Divers brought up statues, pottery, and coins. The ship had sunk sometime around 70 to 60 BCE. Among the finds was a shoebox-sized wooden case, so badly decayed that nobody paid it much attention. Then, in 1902, an archaeologist noticed a gear wheel embedded in one of the fragments. A gear? From ancient Greece? Many scholars assumed it must come from a later period, or that it was a simple navigation instrument. In the 1950s, the historian Derek de Solla Price argued that it was a calculating device, and in the 1970s he used X-rays to count the gear teeth. Then, starting in 2005, researchers used high-resolution CT scanning, which revealed inscriptions hidden inside the fragments, basically a user's manual. Here's what we now know. Turning a handle drove at least thirty interlocking gears, and pointers showed the positions of the sun and moon, the phases of the moon, and the dates of eclipses. One dial even tracked the four-year cycle of athletic games, including the Olympics. That's why it's often called the first analog computer. And here's the strangest part: nothing with comparable gearing appears in the historical record for more than a thousand years, until the astronomical clocks of medieval Europe.

Why the ancient Greeks needed to track the Olympic Games
How medieval clockmakers copied an ancient Greek design
How an ancient geared device was found and gradually understood

explanation: The host traces the device from its discovery in a shipwreck through decades of research into its function.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Today we're looking at a famous book in anthropology, and a famous argument about it. In 1925, a twenty-three-year-old Margaret Mead traveled to the island of Ta'ū in American Samoa. She spent about nine months there, observing and interviewing dozens of adolescent girls. Her question came from a debate back home. Many American psychologists claimed that adolescence was naturally a time of storm and stress, that the emotional turmoil of teenagers was biological. If that were true, Mead reasoned, it should happen everywhere. In her 1928 book, Coming of Age in Samoa, she reported that it didn't. Samoan girls, she wrote, passed through adolescence calmly, with relatively relaxed attitudes about relationships. So the turmoil of American teenagers had to be cultural, not biological. The book became a bestseller. Then, in 1983, five years after Mead died, the anthropologist Derek Freeman published a fierce critique. Freeman had worked in Samoa for years, and he argued that Samoan society actually placed a strong value on virginity and had plenty of conflict and violence. He even suggested that some of Mead's informants had been joking with her. So who was right? Well, most anthropologists today wouldn't simply side with Freeman, either. His fieldwork was done mostly in a different part of Samoa, and decades later, after major social changes. What the controversy really exposed was a problem of method: how much can one researcher, working alone in one place for a few months, claim to know about an entire culture?

A famous study of adolescence and the debate it caused

prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: In 1958, the anthropologist Clifford Geertz and his wife arrived in a small village in Bali to do fieldwork. For about ten days, the villagers treated them as if they didn't exist. Then, one afternoon, the couple attended a cockfight, which was illegal at the time. The police raided it, and everyone ran, including the two anthropologists, who fled alongside the villagers and hid in a courtyard. The next day, the whole village suddenly accepted them. From that fieldwork came his famous 1972 essay, 'Deep Play.' Geertz borrowed two ideas to make sense of the cockfight. The first was thick description, a phrase from the philosopher Gilbert Ryle. Ryle's example was two boys rapidly contracting their right eyelids. For one, it's an involuntary twitch; for the other, it's a wink, a signal to a friend. A camera records the same movement. Only a thick description, one that captures meaning, tells them apart. The second idea, deep play, came from Jeremy Bentham, who used it for bets so high that it's irrational to make them. Geertz noticed two kinds of betting. Side bets between individual spectators were mostly about money. But the large central bet, pooled by groups of allies, was about status. The higher those stakes, the more the fight was really about honor. So, Geertz concluded, the cockfight was a story the Balinese told themselves about themselves. Critics later asked a pointed question, though: whose story? Geertz, they said, rarely asked the participants what they thought.

Ryle's example was two boys rapidly contracting their right eyelids. For one, it's an involuntary twitch; for the other, it's a wink, a signal to a friend. A camera records the same movement. Only a thick description, one that captures meaning, tells them apart. The second idea, deep play, came from Jeremy Bentham, who used it for bets so high that it's irrational to make them. Geertz noticed two kinds of betting. Side bets between individual spectators were mostly about money. But the large central bet, pooled by groups of allies, was about status. The higher those stakes, the more the fight was really about honor. So, Geertz concluded, the cockfight was a story the Balinese told themselves about themselves. Critics later asked a pointed question, though: whose story? Geertz, they said, rarely asked the participants what they thought.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Today: a painter who changed how light works in pictures. Michelangelo Merisi, known as Caravaggio, was born in 1571 and died in 1610, before he turned forty. In that short career, he developed a style we call tenebrism, from the Italian word for darkness. Now, you've heard of chiaroscuro, the contrast of light and shadow. Now, for a long time it was said that Caravaggio never drew, that he painted straight onto the canvas without any preparation. After all, no drawings by him survive. But technical studies have found lines scratched into the wet ground layer of his canvases, marking where figures would go. So he did plan, just not on paper, the way other painters did.

prompt: What is the main topic of the podcast?
audioScript: Today's episode is about how a cheap kind of Japanese print ended up transforming European painting. For over two centuries, Japan had sharply limited contact with the West. Then, in 1854, under pressure from American warships, it signed a treaty opening its ports, and Japanese goods began flowing to Europe. Among them were ukiyo-e, woodblock prints showing actors, landscapes, and city life. Now, each print was a team effort. A designer drew the image. A carver cut it into wooden blocks, a separate block for each color. A printer pressed the paper onto the blocks, one after another. Then a publisher sold them cheaply, like posters. In Japan, these were popular entertainment, not high art. Parisian artists saw them as revelations. After Japan exhibited at the Paris World's Fair of 1867, the craze took off, and by 1872 a critic had a name for it: Japonisme. So what did Europeans take from the prints? Flat areas of bright color, bold outlines, unusual high viewpoints, and figures cut off by the edge of the frame. Compare two painters. Vincent van Gogh copied prints by Hiroshige almost directly, in oil, even painting Japanese characters into the borders. Edgar Degas did something subtler. He borrowed the compositions, the off-center figures and cropped edges, but his subjects stayed entirely Parisian: dancers, racehorses, cafés. And here's the irony. Just as Europe was celebrating these prints as fine art, Japan, eager to modernize, was treating them as disposable and old-fashioned.

How Japanese woodblock prints influenced European artists
Why Japan opened its ports to Western trade in 1854
How Degas and van Gogh worked together on Japanese themes

explanation: The host explains how ukiyo-e reached Europe and how painters such as van Gogh and Degas used them.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Today: sonata form, the structure behind the first movements of most symphonies, sonatas, and string quartets from the classical period, roughly 1750 to 1820. The standard textbook version has three sections. First comes the exposition, which presents two main themes. The first theme is in the home key. Then a transition moves to a new key, usually the dominant, a fifth higher, and the second theme appears there, often more lyrical. The second section is the development. Here the composer breaks the themes into fragments, moves restlessly through different keys, and builds tension. The third section is the recapitulation, where both themes return, but now, crucially, the second theme stays in the home key. That's what resolves the tension. So: exposition, development, recapitulation. Easy to memorize. But here's what textbooks rarely stress. Haydn and Mozart never used the term sonata form. It was coined in the 1840s by theorists like Adolf Bernhard Marx, who described the form mainly in terms of contrasting themes. An earlier theorist, Heinrich Christoph Koch, writing in 1793, during Haydn's lifetime, described the same movements in terms of keys rather than themes: a journey away from home and back again. And Koch's view fits Haydn better. In many of Haydn's movements, the so-called second theme is just the first theme again, in the new key. By Marx's definition, those movements barely qualify. By Koch's, they fit perfectly. So sonata form was a description written after the fact, not a recipe composers followed.

How Mozart and Marx developed the recapitulation together
Why classical composers avoided moving to the dominant key

sampleAnswer: The structure of sonata form and how it has been defined
explanation: The professor describes the three sections of sonata form and compares theme-based and key-based definitions.

prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: Before public concerts, where did people hear music? Mostly in church, at noble courts, and in private homes. If you were a composer, you worked for a patron, a church or a prince, and you wrote what your employer needed. Then, in London in 1672, a violinist named John Banister did something new. He advertised in a newspaper that music would be performed every afternoon at his house, and anyone could attend for a shilling. That's often considered the first series of public concerts with paid admission. Now, compare this with Paris. There, public concerts developed differently. The most important series, the Concert Spirituel, founded in 1725, operated under a royal privilege, and it originally performed on religious holidays when the opera houses were closed. So in Paris, concert life grew under the protection of the crown, while in London it grew as a business. And by the late 1700s, the London market was strong enough for an impresario named Johann Peter Salomon to bring Joseph Haydn over, twice, in the 1790s. Haydn wrote twelve symphonies for those visits, and he wrote them for a paying public. You know the Surprise Symphony, with the sudden loud chord in the quiet slow movement? The famous story is that Haydn wanted to wake up sleeping listeners. He later denied that, saying he simply wanted to do something new and make a brilliant debut. Either way, notice who he was trying to impress: not a prince, but a ticket-buying crowd.

How public concerts emerged and changed composers' audiences
How the Concert Spirituel replaced the Paris opera houses
Why church music declined during the eighteenth century

explanation: The lecturer traces the rise of paid public concerts and how they changed whom composers wrote for.

If you were a composer, you worked for a patron, a church or a prince, and you wrote what your employer needed. Then, in London in 1672, a violinist named John Banister did something new. He advertised in a newspaper that music would be performed every afternoon at his house, and anyone could attend for a shilling. That's often considered the first series of public concerts with paid admission. Now, compare this with Paris. There, public concerts developed differently. The most important series, the Concert Spirituel, founded in 1725, operated under a royal privilege, and it originally performed on religious holidays when the opera houses were closed. So in Paris, concert life grew under the protection of the crown, while in London it grew as a business. And by the late 1700s, the London market was strong enough for an impresario named Johann Peter Salomon to bring Joseph Haydn over, twice, in the 1790s. Haydn wrote twelve symphonies for those visits, and he wrote them for a paying public. You know the Surprise Symphony, with the sudden loud chord in the quiet slow movement? The famous story is that Haydn wanted to wake up sleeping listeners. He later denied that, saying he simply wanted to do something new and make a brilliant debut. Either way, notice who he was trying to impress: not a prince, but a ticket-buying crowd.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Let's talk about the Pantheon in Rome, perhaps the most impressive dome ever built. The building we see today was completed under the emperor Hadrian, around 125 CE, although the inscription on the front credits Agrippa, who built an earlier temple on the site. Now, the numbers. The dome spans about forty-three meters, and the height from the floor to the top is exactly the same, so a perfect sphere would fit inside. At the top is the oculus, an open hole about eight meters across, with no glass. And here's the remarkable part: the dome is unreinforced concrete, no steel at all, and nearly nineteen hundred years later, it's still the largest dome of its kind in the world. So how did the Romans do it? Three strategies. First, they varied the aggregate, the stones mixed into the concrete. Near the base, they used heavy material like travertine; higher up, they switched to lighter volcanic stone, with pumice near the top. Second, the dome's thickness decreases from about six meters at the base to just over one meter at the oculus. Third, the coffers, the sunken ceiling panels, remove even more weight. Compare that with Brunelleschi's dome in Florence, finished in the 1430s. It's slightly wider, but it's built of brick, with two shells, inner and outer. For a long time, people talked about a lost Roman secret. But really, the key was ordinary volcanic ash, which helps concrete set strongly even in damp conditions.

prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: So, why did the skyscraper appear in Chicago in the 1880s? There were really three conditions. The first was a disaster. In 1871, the Great Chicago Fire destroyed much of the city's center, and during rebuilding, land in the business district became very expensive. The economic logic was simple: if land is costly, build up. The second condition was the safety elevator. Elisha Otis had demonstrated one in New York in 1854, with a brake that stopped the car if the cable broke. Without elevators, nobody wanted to climb past five or six floors. But the third condition was the real structural problem. In a traditional building, the walls carry the weight, and the taller you build, the thicker the walls at the bottom have to be. Look at the Monadnock Building in Chicago, completed in 1891. It's sixteen stories tall with load-bearing brick walls, and at the base those walls are about six feet thick. That's about the limit. Now compare the Home Insurance Building, designed by William Le Baron Jenney and completed in 1885. It used an internal metal frame to carry much of the load, so the walls could be thinner. It's usually called the first skyscraper, even though it was only ten stories. But historians argue about that title. Jenney's frame still relied partly on masonry, and others were experimenting too. So the skyscraper wasn't a single invention. It was a gradual shift from walls that hold a building up to a frame that does.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Today we're comparing two versions of the sonnet. Every sonnet has fourteen lines, but how those lines are organized changes how the poem thinks. Start with Petrarch, in fourteenth-century Italy. The Petrarchan sonnet divides into two parts: an octave of eight lines, then a sestet of six. The octave usually rhymes A-B-B-A, A-B-B-A, so it reuses just two rhyme sounds, four times each. And between the octave and the sestet, at line nine, there's a turn, which Italian critics call the volta. The octave raises a problem; the sestet answers or reconsiders it. Now, poets like Thomas Wyatt brought the sonnet to England in the 1530s. But there was a practical difficulty. Italian is full of words with similar endings, so rhymes are easy to find. English has far fewer rhyming words, and finding four rhymes on the same sound, twice, is hard. So English poets gradually developed a different structure: three quatrains of four lines, each with its own new rhymes, and then a final rhyming couplet. When Shakespeare's sonnets were published in 1609, there were a hundred and fifty-four of them, almost all in this form. So where's the turn in the English sonnet? Usually it's delayed until the couplet, which often delivers a sharp twist or summary. That's the standard contrast. But don't apply it too rigidly. Many of Shakespeare's sonnets also shift direction at line nine, just as Petrarch's do. So in practice, the English form often contains two turns, not one.

How Petrarch invented the rhyming couplet

prompt: What is the podcast mainly about?
audioScript: Welcome back. Today: how money shaped the Victorian novel. In the 1830s, a new novel in Britain was usually published in three volumes, and it was very expensive, about a guinea and a half, more than many workers earned in a week. So most readers didn't buy novels. They borrowed them from circulating libraries that charged an annual subscription. Then, in 1836, a young writer named Charles Dickens began publishing The Pickwick Papers in monthly installments. Each part had thirty-two pages and two illustrations, and it cost one shilling. So readers paid a little each month, for about a year and a half. At first, sales were weak; the first part sold only a few hundred copies. But in the fourth installment, Dickens introduced a witty servant named Sam Weller, and sales took off. By the end, each part was selling around forty thousand copies. Now, think about what this format did to writing. A three-volume novel was finished before readers saw it. A serial wasn't. Dickens was often writing just a few weeks ahead of publication, so he could watch sales and readers' letters and adjust his plots. And each installment needed a reason to buy the next one, which encouraged cliffhangers. For a long time, critics treated these features as flaws, saying serial novels were baggy and padded because authors were paid by length. More recently, scholars have argued nearly the opposite: that serialization created a shared, ongoing experience, much like a television series today.

How Dickens created the character of Sam Weller
Why critics have always praised serialized novels
How publishing novels in monthly parts affected readers and writing

sampleAnswer: How publishing novels in monthly parts affected readers and writing
explanation: The host explains how monthly serial publication changed who could buy novels and how they were written.

audioScript: Welcome back. Today: how money shaped the Victorian novel. In the 1830s, a new novel in Britain was usually published in three volumes, and it was very expensive, about a guinea and a half, more than many workers earned in a week. So most readers didn't buy novels. They borrowed them from circulating libraries that charged an annual subscription. Then, in 1836, a young writer named Charles Dickens began publishing The Pickwick Papers in monthly installments. Each part had thirty-two pages and two illustrations, and it cost one shilling. But in the fourth installment, Dickens introduced a witty servant named Sam Weller, and sales took off. By the end, each part was selling around forty thousand copies. prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: A language with no native speakers is usually considered dead. So here's a remarkable case. Hebrew stopped being anyone's everyday spoken language around the second or third century CE. For more than fifteen hundred years after that, it survived, but only in prayer, scholarship, and writing, a bit like Latin in medieval Europe. Then, in 1881, a young man named Eliezer Ben-Yehuda moved to Jerusalem, determined to revive it as a spoken language. He insisted that his family speak only Hebrew at home, and his son, born in 1882, is often called the first native speaker of Hebrew in modern times. He also began a huge dictionary, coining words for modern things. That's the popular story: a single determined man. But historians of language now give much more credit to schools. In the farming settlements of the late 1800s, teachers began teaching all subjects in Hebrew, and children who learned it at school spoke it with each other, and later with their own children. So the revival really happened in three steps: first an ideology, then the classroom, then the homes of the next generation. Compare this with Irish. After Irish independence in 1922, Irish became an official language and was required in schools. Yet today, relatively few use it as their main daily language. One reason: in Palestine, immigrants arrived speaking many different languages, so Hebrew filled a real need as a common language. In Ireland, nearly everyone already shared English.

How Irish became an official language in 1922
Why Latin survived in medieval European scholarship
How Hebrew became a spoken native language again

explanation: The lecturer explains how Hebrew was revived as a spoken language and compares it with Irish.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: In 1967, the British philosopher Philippa Foot published a brief thought experiment. A runaway tram is heading toward five workers on the track. The driver can steer onto a side track, where only one worker stands. Should he? Most people say yes. But Foot paired it with a second case. A judge can stop a deadly riot by framing and executing an innocent man. Again, one life against several, yet almost everyone says no. So what's the difference? Foot drew on distinctions between doing and allowing, and between intending and merely foreseeing. Later, in 1976 and again in 1985, the American philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson pushed the puzzle further and gave it its name, the trolley problem. She introduced two famous variants. In the first, you're a bystander next to a switch, not the driver. In the second, you're on a footbridge above the track, and the only way to stop the trolley is to push a large man off the bridge onto the rails. Surveys consistently show that most people would pull the switch but would not push the man, though the numbers are identical. A common explanation is that pushing uses the man as a means, while switching merely foresees a death as a side effect. But here's a twist. In 2008, Thomson changed her mind. She argued that the bystander, unlike the driver, isn't permitted to switch either, because he'd be imposing a cost on someone else that he wouldn't accept himself.

choices.text: Why judges must never punish people who are innocent
A moral puzzle about sacrificing one life to save several
How trolley drivers are trained to avoid accidents
Why Thomson disagreed with every claim Foot made

sampleAnswer: A moral puzzle about sacrificing one life to save several
explanation: The professor traces the trolley problem from Foot's original cases through Thomson's variants and her later change of mind.

prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: Here's a belief you hold with complete confidence: the sun will rise tomorrow. Why? Because it has risen every day so far. That kind of reasoning, from past cases to future ones, is called induction. In 1739, the Scottish philosopher David Hume asked a devastating question: what justifies it? Hume's argument works in two steps. Induction assumes that the future will resemble the past, that nature is uniform. So, step one: can we prove that assumption by pure logic? No. There's no contradiction in imagining that tomorrow the sun doesn't rise. It would be surprising, but it isn't logically impossible, the way a square circle is. Step two: can we prove it from experience? We could say the future has always resembled the past before. But that's itself an inductive argument. We'd be using induction to justify induction, which is circular. So Hume concluded that our expectations rest not on reason but on custom, or habit. After seeing one thing follow another many times, the mind simply expects it. Bertrand Russell later made the point vividly with a chicken. Fed every day, it confidently expects food, until the day the farmer wrings its neck instead. In the twentieth century, Karl Popper accepted Hume's argument but denied that science needs induction at all. Scientists, he said, don't prove theories from repeated observations; they propose bold theories and try to refute them. No number of fed days proves a theory, but one wrung neck can disprove it.

We'd be using induction to justify induction, which is circular. So Hume concluded that our expectations rest not on reason but on custom, or habit. After seeing one thing follow another many times, the mind simply expects it. Bertrand Russell later made the point vividly with a chicken. In the twentieth century, Karl Popper accepted Hume's argument but denied that science needs induction at all. Scientists, he said, don't prove theories from repeated observations; they propose bold theories and try to refute them. No number of fed days proves a theory, but one wrung neck can disprove it.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: Before the 1880s, most people assumed memory was too complex to measure scientifically. Then a German psychologist, Hermann Ebbinghaus, decided to try, using the only subject he had complete access to: himself. His key problem was that real words come with associations. If you learn the word 'apple,' it connects to everything you already know. So he invented over two thousand nonsense syllables, things like 'dax' or 'bok,' consonant, vowel, consonant, with no meaning at all. Then he memorized lists of them perfectly and tested himself after different delays. He didn't just ask, how many can I recall? He measured savings: how much less time it took to relearn the list compared with the first time. Even if you can't recall a single item, relearning might be faster, which shows something remained. His 1885 results produced what's called the forgetting curve. The drop is steep at first. Within about an hour, more than half the savings were gone. After a day, about two thirds. But then the curve flattens, so that a month later, he still retained around a fifth. He also found that spreading practice over several days was more efficient than cramming it into one session. Now, compare nonsense syllables with meaningful material. Ebbinghaus also memorized stanzas of a poem by Byron, and those took roughly a tenth of the effort. That points to a real limitation. The very thing that made his method precise, removing meaning, also made it unlike most real-world memory.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: In 1932, the British psychologist Frederic Bartlett published a book called Remembering, taking a different approach from earlier memory research, which often used meaningless material to keep things controlled. Bartlett thought that missed the point. Real memory, he argued, is all about meaning. So he gave his participants, students at Cambridge, a Native American folk tale called 'The War of the Ghosts.' To a British reader, it's a strange story: two young men hunting seals hear war cries, join a war party in canoes, and one realizes his companions are ghosts. Bartlett used two methods. In repeated reproduction, the same person retold the story several times, after delays of minutes, months, even years. In serial reproduction, one person's version was passed to a second person, who retold it to a third, a bit like the children's game of telephone. Both methods produced the same kinds of changes. The story got shorter. Unfamiliar details were replaced with familiar ones: canoes became boats, and hunting seals became fishing. And the supernatural element, the ghosts, was often explained away or forgotten. Bartlett explained this with the concept of a schema, organized knowledge that shapes how we take in and recall information. We don't replay memories like a recording; we rebuild them using what we already expect. Now, a caveat. His instructions were informal, and some later researchers who asked participants to be as accurate as possible found fewer distortions. Still, his central claim, that remembering is reconstruction, is now widely accepted.

How the children's game of telephone was invented
How a study showed that memory reconstructs information
Why memory research should use meaningless material

explanation: The professor explains Bartlett's experiments and his conclusion that remembering is reconstruction.

prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: Suicide seems like the most individual act imaginable. That's exactly why the French sociologist Émile Durkheim chose to study it. In his 1897 book, Suicide, he wanted to show that even this decision has social causes. He compared official statistics across countries and groups and found stable patterns. Suicide rates were higher among Protestants than Catholics, higher among unmarried people than married people, and, interestingly, they fell during wars and political crises. Individual psychology couldn't explain why whole groups differed so consistently, year after year. So Durkheim proposed two social forces. The first is integration, how strongly people are bound into a group. Too little integration produces what he called egoistic suicide. Protestantism, he argued, encouraged individual judgment and integrated people less than Catholicism. Too much integration, where the individual barely matters compared with the group, produces altruistic suicide, like a soldier sacrificing himself. The second force is regulation, how much society limits people's desires. Too little produces anomic suicide, from the word anomie, meaning normlessness. Strikingly, rates rose not only during economic crashes but also during sudden booms. Any rapid change loosens the rules that tell people what to expect. Too much regulation produces fatalistic suicide, which he barely discussed. Critics later raised a problem. Official statistics depend on who records a death as suicide. Where suicide carried strong religious stigma, as in many Catholic areas, families and officials may have reported fewer cases. So some of Durkheim's patterns may partly reflect recording, not reality.

How Catholic communities recorded official statistics
Why individual psychology explains suicide best

explanation: The lecturer presents Durkheim's use of statistics and his theory of integration and regulation.

prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: In 1958, a New Zealand-born economist working in London, A. W. Phillips, published a study of British data covering nearly a century, from 1861 to 1957. He found a strikingly consistent relationship: when unemployment was low, wages rose quickly, and when unemployment was high, wages rose slowly or even fell. In 1960, the American economists Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow restated the idea in terms of prices. Plotting US data, they suggested a tradeoff between inflation and unemployment. Policymakers loved this, because it looked like a menu. Want lower unemployment? Accept a bit more inflation. Then, in 1968, Milton Friedman argued that the menu was an illusion, at least in the long run. His reasoning went in stages. Suppose the government stimulates the economy and inflation rises. At first, workers don't expect the higher inflation, so they accept wage offers that look generous, and unemployment falls. But in the second stage, workers notice that prices have risen, and they start demanding higher wages to keep up. Firms hire less, and unemployment drifts back to what Friedman called its natural rate. Now the economy has the same unemployment as before, but higher inflation. The 1970s seemed to confirm this. Many Western economies suffered high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, so-called stagflation, which the simple curve said shouldn't happen. Today, economists still use a Phillips curve, but one in which expectations play a central role. The tradeoff exists, but only temporarily.

choices.text: How Phillips collected wage data in New Zealand
Why governments in the 1970s stopped measuring inflation
How economists' view of the inflation-unemployment tradeoff changed
Why workers prefer higher wages to lower unemployment

sampleAnswer: How economists' view of the inflation-unemployment tradeoff changed
explanation: The lecturer traces the Phillips curve from Phillips's data through Friedman's critique and stagflation.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: In January 1914, the Ford Motor Company announced something that stunned American industry: it would pay workers five dollars a day. At the time, Ford's typical wage was about two dollars and thirty-four cents for a nine-hour day, so this roughly doubled pay, and it cut the workday to eight hours. Why? Let's go back one year. In 1913, Ford introduced the moving assembly line at its Highland Park plant. Productivity soared. But the work was monotonous and exhausting, and workers quit in huge numbers. Turnover that year reached about three hundred seventy percent. In other words, to keep a workforce of around fourteen thousand people, the company had to hire more than fifty thousand over the year. Every new worker had to be trained, and every departure slowed the line. So the five-dollar day was a business decision. And it worked. After it was introduced, turnover dropped dramatically and absenteeism fell. Henry Ford later called it one of the finest cost-cutting moves the company ever made. Economists call this an efficiency wage: paying above the market rate because it raises productivity. Now, there's a popular story that Ford raised wages so workers could afford to buy Ford cars. That might have been a small bonus, but most historians doubt it was the main reason. Ford's own workers were a tiny fraction of its customers. And there was a catch. To qualify, workers had to meet standards of personal behavior, checked by company investigators who visited their homes.

Why Ford wanted all of its workers to buy Ford cars

prompt: What is the podcast mainly about?
audioScript: Today: how Toyota changed the way factories think about inventory. After World War Two, American companies like Ford relied on mass production: make huge numbers of identical parts, store them in warehouses, and push them down the line, just in case they're needed. That requires lots of space and lots of capital, and Toyota had neither. An engineer named Taiichi Ohno, working from the late 1940s on, came up with an alternative. His inspiration, reportedly, was the American supermarket. In a supermarket, shelves aren't filled based on a forecast. A customer takes a can of soup, and only then does the store restock that can. So Ohno reversed the flow. Instead of pushing parts forward, each step pulls parts from the step before, only when needed. The signal was a simple card called a kanban. When a box of parts was used up, its card went back to the previous process, ordering exactly that many more. This became known as just-in-time production. A second idea was even older. In the 1920s, Sakichi Toyoda, the father of Toyota's founder, had invented a loom that stopped automatically when a thread broke. Ohno extended this: any worker could stop the entire line on spotting a defect. That sounds wasteful, but it meant problems were fixed immediately, not built into hundreds of cars. Now, just-in-time has a weakness. With almost no inventory, a single disruption can halt production. After the 2011 earthquake in Japan, Toyota itself began keeping larger stockpiles of critical parts.

Why American supermarkets kept large stockpiles of goods
How Ford adopted kanban cards in its own factories
Why the 2011 earthquake ended just-in-time production

sampleAnswer: How Toyota developed a production system with little inventory
explanation: The host explains Ohno's just-in-time system, its origins, and its weakness.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: If you've taken a teacher-training course, you've probably seen a colorful pyramid labeled Bloom's taxonomy. But its real story is different from the pyramid. In 1956, a team led by the educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom published a framework that classified learning goals into six levels. From bottom to top: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. The idea was that each level builds on the ones below it. You can't analyze something you don't comprehend. Now, here's the part people forget. The original purpose wasn't to guide teaching at all. It was to help university examiners. Examiners at different universities wanted to share test questions, and needed a common vocabulary for what each question measured. And the original handbook had no pyramid; that came later. Then, in 2001, a group including several of Bloom's former students and colleagues published a revision. They made two important changes. First, they turned the nouns into verbs: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create. That emphasized what learners actually do. Second, they swapped the top two levels. Synthesis, now renamed create, moved to the very top, above evaluate. Their reasoning was that producing something new is generally more demanding than judging something that already exists. Some educators have questioned the hierarchy itself, though. The pyramid makes remembering look like the least important level. But you can't evaluate an argument about history without knowing a good deal of history. So critics argue that the lower levels aren't less valuable, just more basic.

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: On the evening of October 30, 1938, the night before Halloween, CBS radio broadcast an adaptation of H. G. Wells's novel The War of the Worlds, produced by Orson Welles and his Mercury Theatre company. The clever twist was the format. Instead of simply narrating the story, the first part was presented as a series of news bulletins interrupting a music program: reports of explosions on Mars, then a strange object landing at a farm in Grovers Mill, New Jersey, then creatures emerging and attacking. The next morning, newspapers across the country carried headlines about mass panic: people fleeing their homes, jamming phone lines, crowding the roads. And in 1940, a Princeton researcher named Hadley Cantril published a study estimating that about six million people had heard the broadcast and more than a million had been frightened. For decades, it served as the classic example of media power. More recent historians have looked again, and the picture has changed. First, the audience was small. A ratings survey that night found only about two percent of respondents listening to the program; most people were tuned to a popular comedy show on another network. Second, the newspaper reports were mostly based on anecdotes, and many were quickly exaggerated. Why? Radio was their fast-growing competitor for advertising money, and a story about radio's irresponsibility served their interests. So, some people were frightened, certainly. But the mass panic was, to a large extent, a media creation itself, just not by radio.

intro: Listen to a talk in a media studies class.

prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
audioScript: In New York in the early 1830s, a daily newspaper usually meant a mercantile paper, full of shipping news, commodity prices, and political speeches. It cost six cents a copy, but usually you couldn't buy single copies; you paid an annual subscription of around ten dollars, more than many workers earned in a week. These papers were aimed at merchants and politicians, and many survived on support from political parties. Then, on September 3, 1833, a young printer named Benjamin Day launched the New York Sun, priced at one penny. Day changed three things at once. First, distribution: instead of subscriptions, boys sold the paper on street corners, one copy at a time. Second, content: instead of shipping lists, the Sun ran crime reports, stories from the police court, and human-interest tales about ordinary people. And third, the business model. At one cent, the paper couldn't make money from sales alone. Profit came from advertisers paying to reach a huge audience. Within a few years, the Sun had one of the largest circulations in the world. In 1835, it even ran articles claiming a famous astronomer had found creatures on the Moon, and sales jumped. So how should we judge the penny press? Historians used to see it mainly as the birth of sensationalism, and the Moon story supports that. But many now emphasize something else: by depending on advertisers and readers rather than parties, newspapers became more independent of politics, and news became something meant for everyone.

Why the Sun stopped publishing stories about the Moon
How merchants used newspapers to set shipping prices

prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
audioScript: So, for the first half of the twentieth century, biologists believed that ordinary animal cells, given the right nutrients, could keep dividing in a dish forever. That belief came largely from a French surgeon, Alexis Carrel, who claimed he'd kept chicken heart cells growing for more than thirty years. In nineteen sixty-one, a researcher named Leonard Hayflick showed it wasn't true. Human fetal cells in his cultures divided roughly forty to sixty times, and then they just stopped. They didn't die; they entered a permanent retirement we call senescence. That ceiling became known as the Hayflick limit. But what was counting the divisions? The answer lies at the tips of our chromosomes, in structures called telomeres. A telomere is a short DNA sequence repeated over a thousand times, a bit like the plastic cap on a shoelace. Now, here's the mechanism, in three steps. First, every time a cell copies its DNA, the copying machinery can't quite reach the very end of the strand. Second, so with each division, the telomere gets shorter. Third, once it falls below a critical length, the cell reads that as damage and stops dividing. So why don't the cells that make sperm and eggs run out? They use an enzyme called telomerase, which rebuilds the caps. And cancer cells? Roughly eighty-five to ninety percent of them switch telomerase back on, which is partly why they divide indefinitely. As for Carrel's chicken cells? Most likely, fresh cells were added each time the cultures were fed.

How cancer cells repair the damaged ends of their DNA before each new division
Why chicken cells survive longer in culture than human cells
How telomerase was first discovered in reproductive cells

prompt: According to the professor, what did Hayflick observe in his cell cultures?
audioScript: So, for the first half of the twentieth century, biologists believed that ordinary animal cells, given the right nutrients, could keep dividing in a dish forever. That belief came largely from a French surgeon, Alexis Carrel, who claimed he'd kept chicken heart cells growing for more than thirty years. They didn't die; they entered a permanent retirement we call senescence. That ceiling became known as the Hayflick limit. But what was counting the divisions? Now, here's the mechanism, in three steps. First, every time a cell copies its DNA, the copying machinery can't quite reach the very end of the strand. Second, so with each division, the telomere gets shorter. Third, once it falls below a critical length, the cell reads that as damage and stops dividing. So why don't the cells that make sperm and eggs run out? They use an enzyme called telomerase, which rebuilds the caps. And cancer cells? Roughly eighty-five to ninety percent of them switch telomerase back on, which is partly why they divide indefinitely. As for Carrel's chicken cells? Most likely, fresh cells were added each time the cultures were fed.
