prompt: Dr. Abebe: Generative artificial intelligence tools can now produce essays, summarize readings, and suggest revisions within seconds. Universities have responded in very different ways. Some prohibit these tools in written assignments, viewing their use as a form of academic dishonesty. Others permit or even encourage them, provided students disclose how they were used, arguing that graduates will rely on such technology throughout their careers. Should universities allow students to use AI tools when completing writing assignments? If so, under what conditions? Explain your view.
passage:
Sienna: Universities should permit AI tools with clear disclosure rules. Prohibiting them is nearly impossible to enforce, and it leaves students unprepared for workplaces where these tools are already standard. Instructors could redesign assignments to emphasize analysis and personal reflection, while students learn to evaluate and improve AI-generated drafts critically, which is itself a valuable skill.

Gabriel: I believe AI tools should generally be prohibited in writing assignments. Writing is not merely a way of producing text; it is a way of thinking. When students struggle to organize an argument, they develop their reasoning abilities. If software performs that work, students may earn good grades without ever learning to think clearly on their own.
sampleAnswer: I agree with Sienna that universities should allow AI tools, but I believe the conditions should depend on the purpose of each assignment. Gabriel makes an important point that writing develops thinking, and for that reason, introductory courses designed to teach argument construction might reasonably restrict these tools. In advanced courses, however, permitting them under disclosure rules seems more realistic. My additional argument is that a clear policy encourages honesty. When tools are completely banned, students who use them anyway have every incentive to hide it, and instructors cannot discuss responsible use. When usage is permitted and documented, instructors can see exactly how students relied on the technology and offer guidance. In one of my courses, students submitted their AI-generated outline alongside a reflection explaining which suggestions they rejected and why. This process revealed the quality of our reasoning more effectively than a conventional essay alone.

prompt: Dr. Kowalski: For much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, historians concentrated on political leaders, military campaigns, and major treaties. Beginning in the mid-twentieth century, social historians shifted attention toward ordinary people: farmers, factory workers, families, and migrants whose experiences had been largely absent from official records. Today, both approaches coexist, but scholars still debate which offers the more meaningful account of the past. In your opinion, should history education place greater emphasis on major events and influential leaders or on the everyday lives of ordinary people? Support your answer.
passage:
Clara: I believe history education should emphasize major events and leaders. Decisions made by governments, such as declaring independence or signing trade agreements, affected millions of people at once. Without understanding these turning points, students cannot grasp why societies developed as they did. Everyday life is interesting, but it makes sense only within that larger political framework.

Desmond: I would emphasize ordinary people. Focusing on leaders gives students the misleading impression that history is shaped by a handful of individuals. In reality, large-scale changes like industrialization or urbanization resulted from countless decisions by workers and families. Studying their lives also helps students see themselves as participants in history rather than spectators.
sampleAnswer: Although Clara convincingly argues that major decisions shape entire societies, I agree with Desmond that history education should place greater emphasis on ordinary people. My primary reason is that the lives of ordinary people reveal how large events were experienced, which is often quite different from how they were officially described. A government might announce a new agricultural policy as a triumph, yet diaries and local records could show that farming families endured hardship as a result. Without such perspectives, students may accept official narratives uncritically. In addition, social history allows students to investigate questions using evidence close to home. My class once examined census records and photographs from our own town to trace how women's employment changed over several decades. That project made abstract concepts like economic modernization tangible. Major events still matter, but they become far more meaningful when examined through the experiences of the people they affected.

prompt: Dr. Herrera: Philosophers have long debated whether honesty is an absolute duty or whether it may be outweighed by other values, such as kindness. Consider everyday situations: a friend asks your opinion of a business plan you find unrealistic, or a colleague asks whether a presentation went well when it clearly did not. Some argue that complete candor, delivered respectfully, ultimately serves people best. Others maintain that softening or withholding unwelcome truths is sometimes the more ethical choice. When giving feedback to friends or colleagues, should people always be fully honest, or are there circumstances in which kindness should take priority? Explain your position.
passage:
Zara: Full honesty should be the rule. If I tell a friend that a flawed business plan is excellent, I may cause her to lose money and time. Kindness that hides important information is really a form of disrespect, because it assumes the other person cannot handle the truth. Honest feedback can be delivered gently without being distorted.

Leo: Kindness should sometimes take priority. Timing and context matter enormously. If a colleague has just finished a presentation and is visibly upset, pointing out every weakness immediately serves no purpose and may damage the relationship. Sometimes it's more ethical to offer encouragement in the moment and reserve detailed criticism for later, or for situations where it can genuinely help.
sampleAnswer: I largely agree with Zara that honesty should be the guiding principle, but Leo's emphasis on timing reveals an important nuance. I think the ethical question is less about whether to tell the truth and more about how and when to communicate it. Delaying criticism until someone is ready to hear it differs fundamentally from deceiving them. Moreover, dishonest reassurance often undermines the very relationships it seeks to protect. If a friend later discovers that I praised a plan I privately doubted, she may begin to question all of my future compliments, making my support meaningless. For example, when a classmate asked me to review his scholarship essay, I pointed out that its opening was unfocused while also highlighting its genuinely moving conclusion. He revised it and was grateful precisely because he trusted my assessment. Kindness, therefore, should shape the delivery of feedback rather than replace its content.

prompt: Dr. Chen: Since remote work became widespread, sociologists have begun examining its effects on local communities. Ines: Remote work has strengthened neighborhood communities. When people commuted, residential areas were nearly empty during the day. sampleAnswer: I find Oscar's position somewhat more persuasive, although Ines describes a genuine benefit for certain neighborhoods. My additional concern is that remote work reduces exposure to people unlike ourselves. Neighborhoods tend to be relatively homogeneous in terms of income and lifestyle, whereas workplaces bring together colleagues of different ages, cultures, and backgrounds. A cousin of mine who started a remote job after graduating spent months knowing almost no one in her new city. prompt: Dr. Duval: Traditional letter grades have been a fixture of higher education for over a century, but some institutions are experimenting with alternatives. These include pass/fail systems, in which students either meet course requirements or do not, and narrative evaluations, in which instructors write detailed comments describing each student's strengths and areas for growth. Advocates claim these alternatives reduce destructive competition and encourage intellectual risk-taking. Skeptics contend that they make it harder for employers and graduate programs to compare applicants. Should universities replace traditional letter grades with pass/fail or narrative evaluations? Explain your reasoning.
passage:
Naomi: Universities should move away from letter grades. Students today are so focused on protecting their grade point average that they avoid challenging courses outside their expertise. Narrative evaluations would encourage genuine curiosity and give students far more useful feedback than a single letter. A comment explaining how to strengthen an argument teaches much more than a B-minus.

Arjun: Letter grades should remain. They provide a clear, standardized signal that employers and admissions committees can interpret quickly. Without them, decision-makers may rely more heavily on factors like the prestige of a student's university or personal connections, which would disadvantage students from less privileged backgrounds. Grades, despite their flaws, offer a relatively objective measure.
sampleAnswer: Although Naomi presents an appealing vision of curiosity-driven learning, I agree with Arjun that letter grades should remain the primary system. His point about prestige is crucial: when standardized measures disappear, evaluators tend to substitute other signals, and those signals frequently favor students who already enjoy advantages. I would add that narrative evaluations raise practical concerns about consistency. Instructors differ enormously in their writing styles, and some are naturally generous with praise while others are reserved, so two equally capable students might receive descriptions that sound very different. Grades are imperfect, yet a common scale at least reduces this variation. That said, I believe universities could address Naomi's concern without eliminating grades entirely. Many institutions allow students to take one or two elective courses on a pass/fail basis, which encourages exploration while preserving reliable records. This compromise seems to combine the strengths of both approaches.

prompt: Dr. Park: Hiring practices vary considerably across organizations. Some employers prioritize demonstrated skills and experience, selecting candidates who can contribute effectively from their first day. Others emphasize potential, choosing applicants who may lack specific qualifications but show adaptability, curiosity, and a capacity for learning, and then investing in their training. Proponents of the latter approach argue that technical skills quickly become outdated in rapidly changing industries. When filling an important position, should companies prioritize candidates' current skills and experience or their long-term potential? Justify your view.
passage:
Hugo: Companies should prioritize proven skills and experience. Training inexperienced employees is costly and time-consuming, and there is no guarantee that potential will translate into actual performance. An experienced candidate has a track record that can be verified through references and past results, which significantly reduces the risk of a poor hiring decision for an important role.

Lina: Potential should be the priority. In industries like technology or marketing, the tools used today may be obsolete within five years, so an employee's ability to learn matters more than current expertise. Candidates selected for potential also tend to be highly motivated and loyal, since they appreciate the company's investment in their development.
sampleAnswer: While Hugo is right that experience reduces short-term risk, I am persuaded by Lina's argument that companies should prioritize long-term potential, particularly in rapidly evolving industries. Experience demonstrates what a candidate has accomplished under past conditions, but it reveals relatively little about how that person will respond to unfamiliar challenges. My additional reason is that hiring exclusively for experience can make organizations less diverse in their thinking. If every new employee comes from similar roles at competing firms, the company tends to replicate established practices rather than develop fresh approaches. Candidates with unconventional backgrounds often notice inefficiencies that industry veterans take for granted. For example, a friend of mine was hired by a logistics company after studying biology, and her experience with laboratory data led her to redesign the firm's inventory tracking system. Experience certainly matters, yet adaptability is what sustains an organization's performance over time.

prompt: Dr. Quinn: Ecotourism, defined as responsible travel to natural areas that supports conservation and local well-being, has expanded dramatically in recent decades. Advocates argue that it gives local communities a financial incentive to protect forests, reefs, and wildlife rather than exploit them, while educating visitors about environmental issues. Critics counter that growing numbers of tourists inevitably disturb wildlife, generate waste, and require roads and lodging that degrade the very environments they come to admire. On balance, do you believe ecotourism does more to protect or to harm fragile ecosystems? Explain your reasoning.
passage:
Camila: Ecotourism does more good than harm. Without tourism income, communities near rainforests often have little choice but to log or clear land for agriculture. When tourists pay to see intact ecosystems, preserving them becomes economically rational. Park entrance fees also fund rangers and research that governments might otherwise be unable to afford.

Nathan: I believe ecotourism ultimately causes more harm. Its popularity is self-defeating: as a destination becomes famous, visitor numbers grow beyond what the environment can support. Wildlife changes its behavior to avoid crowds, trails erode, and hotels strain local water supplies. Furthermore, the label ecotourism is often applied loosely to businesses with minimal environmental commitments.
sampleAnswer: I believe ecotourism does more to protect fragile ecosystems, provided it is properly regulated, and in this respect I agree with Camila's argument about economic incentives. Nathan correctly warns that popularity can become self-defeating, but I see this as a problem of management rather than an inherent flaw. Destinations that cap daily visitor numbers, require licensed guides, and restrict construction have demonstrated that tourism and conservation can coexist. My additional point concerns the alternatives. If a forest generates no tourism income, it is rarely left untouched; more often, it faces pressure from mining, logging, or large-scale agriculture, all of which cause far more permanent damage than visitors on guided trails. Moreover, ecotourism creates a constituency of people who have personally witnessed these ecosystems and are therefore more likely to support their protection after returning home. Responsible tourism is often the most realistic way to make conservation financially sustainable.

prompt: Dr. Osei: Sleep researchers have found that adolescents' internal clocks shift during puberty, making it biologically difficult for many teenagers to fall asleep before eleven at night. Nevertheless, numerous high schools begin classes before eight in the morning, and chronic sleep deprivation among teenagers has been linked to poorer academic performance, mood problems, and car accidents. Some school districts have delayed start times, but opponents point to complications involving bus schedules, after-school sports, and parents' work hours. Should high schools adopt later start times to accommodate adolescent sleep patterns? Explain your position.
passage:
Maya: High schools should definitely start later. The scientific evidence is compelling, and it would be unreasonable to ignore students' biology for the sake of convenience. Districts that have shifted start times have reported improvements in attendance and alertness. The logistical challenges with buses and sports are real, but they are solvable problems, whereas sleep deprivation harms students' health directly.

Ryan: I'm skeptical that later start times are the right solution. If school begins later, it ends later, which pushes sports, part-time jobs, and homework further into the evening. Many teenagers might simply go to bed later still, eliminating the benefit. Schools would achieve more by educating families about limiting screen use at night and maintaining consistent sleep schedules.
sampleAnswer: I support later start times, and I find Maya's argument more convincing than Ryan's, though Ryan raises a reasonable concern about evening schedules. The crucial distinction is that education about screen use, while valuable, asks teenagers to override a biological shift that the research describes as genuinely difficult to resist. Expecting individual willpower to overcome biology seems less realistic than adjusting an institutional schedule. My additional reason concerns fairness. Students from families with flexible resources can compensate for early start times, for instance by being driven to school rather than catching a bus before dawn. Students without those options bear the full burden of sleep loss, which may widen existing gaps in academic achievement. As for Ryan's worry that teenagers will simply stay up later, studies of districts that changed their schedules found that students gained sleep overall. Therefore, although implementation requires careful planning, the health benefits justify the change.

Keira: Chronological feeds should be the default. Algorithms are designed to maximize the time users spend on a platform, not their well-being. Transparency like this builds healthier online habits.

Mateo: I don't think chronological feeds should be the default. With an algorithmic feed, content never runs out, which encourages the compulsive scrolling Keira mentions. When I switched one of my accounts to chronological order, I found that I checked it less frequently and ended each session feeling informed rather than drained. prompt: Dr. Hartley: In our lab section this semester, we have been studying the anatomy of vertebrates, and many of you have asked about dissection. passage:
Alicia: I think virtual dissection is the better choice for introductory courses. With software, I can repeat a dissection as many times as I need, rotate organs, and hide or show different body systems. In a real lab, if I make a wrong cut, the specimen is damaged and I cannot go back. Most students in an intro course are not going to be surgeons, so they mainly need to understand how the systems connect.

Brandon: I disagree. When I dissected a frog in high school, I was surprised by how small and delicate the organs actually were, something a screen never showed me. Handling real tissue builds practical skills that future nurses, vets, and researchers will really need.
sampleAnswer: Although Brandon makes a good point about the value of hands-on experience, I agree with Alicia that introductory courses should switch to virtual dissection. For beginners, the main goal is to understand how organ systems work together, and software does this very effectively. Another reason that neither classmate mentioned is cost. Preserved specimens must be purchased every semester, and they require chemicals, ventilation, and safe disposal. A university could invest that money once in software licenses and use the savings to hire more teaching assistants or buy better microscopes. Finally, some students feel uncomfortable around preserved animals and become too distracted to learn. Virtual tools allow everyone to focus on the actual biology. For these reasons, I believe virtual dissection is the smarter choice at the introductory level.

Tessa: I believe higher prices would be more effective. Money is a powerful motivator, and when people see a large bill, they immediately start turning off lights and using air conditioning less. Umar: I think information works better. Most people simply don't know which appliances use the most electricity. When prices rise, families may cut back temporarily but return to old habits once they get used to higher bills. In contrast, when a family learns that a specific appliance wastes energy and replaces it, the savings continue for years. prompt: Dr. Ibrahim: In this course, we have traced the history of space exploration from the first satellites to today's missions to Mars and beyond. Vanessa: I think agencies should focus on robots. A single human mission to Mars could cost as much as dozens of robotic missions. Wesley: I believe human missions deserve more focus. A rover can take weeks to drive a short distance because scientists on Earth have to plan every movement. sampleAnswer: I agree with Vanessa that space agencies should focus mainly on robotic missions. In addition to the cost savings Vanessa mentioned, robotic missions allow agencies to explore distant places that humans simply cannot reach in a lifetime. For instance, the Voyager probes have traveled beyond the edge of our solar system, and other spacecraft have studied the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn. These destinations would take many years to reach, making human missions impractical. Focusing on robots therefore lets scientists study a much greater variety of worlds. Human missions may become more realistic in the future, but for now, robots provide far more scientific knowledge for each dollar spent.

passage:
Ximena: I think visualizations are more effective. Most people are busy and won't read several paragraphs about statistics. Yusuf: I'd argue that written summaries are more reliable. Many people don't know how to read charts correctly. Another advantage that hasn't been mentioned is that visualizations overcome language barriers. In a diverse city, many residents may not read the official language fluently, so a long written report could exclude them. A clear map showing which neighborhoods have the worst air quality can be understood by almost anyone, regardless of their reading level or native language. Visuals are also easier to share on social media, so important findings reach more people. For these reasons, I believe a well-designed chart, perhaps supported by a brief caption, is the most effective way to communicate data to the public.

prompt: Dr. Petrov: Advances in genetic engineering have made a once-fictional idea seem possible: de-extinction, or bringing back species such as the woolly mammoth or the passenger pigeon by editing the genomes of their closest living relatives. Supporters argue that revived species could restore lost ecological functions and that the research will produce tools useful for saving endangered species. Critics counter that the costs are enormous, that revived animals would lack suitable habitats, and that the same money could protect thousands of species that still exist today. Should research funding be directed toward de-extinction projects, or should it be devoted entirely to conserving existing species? Defend your position.
passage:
Ivy: I think de-extinction research deserves some funding, though not a large share. The genetic techniques developed for mammoths, such as editing genes for cold tolerance, could later help endangered species adapt to changing climates. In that sense, the research isn't really competing with conservation; it may become one of its tools. Also, much of the current funding comes from private investors who wouldn't otherwise donate to traditional conservation programs.

Kenji: I understand the scientific appeal, but I believe funding should go to existing species. Even if scientists produce a mammoth-like animal, it would essentially be a genetically modified elephant raised without parents of its own kind, so it couldn't learn natural behaviors. sampleAnswer: This is a difficult question, but I side with Kenji that public conservation funding should focus on existing species. Ivy makes a thoughtful point that the genetic tools may eventually benefit endangered animals; however, if that is the real goal, it would be more efficient to fund those tools directly for living species rather than through costly projects to recreate extinct ones. A further concern is what economists call moral hazard. If the public comes to believe that extinction is reversible, governments and industries may feel less pressure to prevent it in the first place. A developer, for instance, might argue that destroying a rare frog's wetland is acceptable because scientists could simply bring the species back later. Even a small shift in attitudes like this could cause far more harm than de-extinction could ever repair. Therefore, although the science is fascinating, I believe conservation budgets should protect the species we still have.

prompt: Dr. Ramirez: In our unit on biological invasions, we have seen how species introduced by humans, such as rats on islands or certain fish in lakes, can drive native species toward extinction. Miles: I think we need to be more flexible. Ecosystems are always changing, and returning to some historical baseline is often unrealistic. In parts of the southwestern United States, an endangered bird nests in introduced tamarisk trees, so removing them could actually harm a native species. Rather than automatic eradication, managers should evaluate each case and act only when an invasive species is causing clear and serious harm.
sampleAnswer: I find Miles's case-by-case approach more convincing, although Lucia is right that eradication can produce remarkable results, as her seabird example shows. The key difference is that island rats are a clearly destructive threat, while many long-established species have become tangled in complex relationships that scientists do not fully understand. Removing them can trigger unexpected chain reactions. For instance, when cats were eliminated from Macquarie Island in Australia, the rabbit population exploded and destroyed much of the island's vegetation, which then required another costly eradication campaign. This example shows that removing one species can make problems worse if managers do not consider the entire food web. In addition, conservation budgets are limited, so money spent fighting a species that is now relatively harmless could instead protect habitats under urgent threat. Therefore, I believe managers should carefully assess each situation rather than eradicating every introduced species by default.

Investing in diverse crops could address this hidden hunger while making farms more adaptable to climate change. Moreover, seeds stored in banks are not adapted to new conditions unless researchers actively work with them. For these reasons, diversity deserves priority.

Rafael: I'd lean toward preparedness, even though chronic disease causes more deaths in an average year. sampleAnswer: I agree with Rafael that pandemic preparedness deserves a larger share of the budget, although Pia is right that chronic disease causes more deaths in a typical year. If the national agency does not fund these systems, nobody will. Furthermore, Pia's concern about expiring supplies can be addressed by rotating stockpiled items into regular hospital use before they expire. Since the agency is uniquely responsible for preparedness while chronic disease has multiple supporters, I believe directing more funding toward pandemic readiness is the wiser choice.

prompt: Dr. Zhou: This week we examined adaptive reuse, the practice of converting old buildings, such as factories, warehouses, or schools, for new purposes like apartments, offices, or museums. Cora: I think it depends, but replacement is often the better choice. Some old buildings are so inefficient that heating them wastes energy every single day. sampleAnswer: I agree with Bruno that cities should generally encourage adaptive reuse, although Cora is correct that some buildings are simply too inefficient or unsafe to save. Iris: I'd prioritize distributed generation. Large projects often face years of delays because new transmission lines require permits, and local communities frequently oppose them. Only utility-scale projects, combined with large battery facilities, can meet this demand at an affordable price. That said, Iris's point about resilience is valuable, so I would target distributed solar and batteries at critical sites like hospitals, emergency shelters, and remote communities. prompt: Dr. Ellison: In machine learning, there is often a trade-off between accuracy and interpretability. Complex models, such as deep neural networks, can make highly accurate predictions, but even their designers cannot fully explain why a particular decision was made. This trade-off becomes important when algorithms help make decisions about people, such as approving loans, screening job applicants, or predicting which patients need extra care. passage:
Lars: Yes, I think explainability should be required for decisions about people. If a bank denies someone a loan, that person deserves to know why and to have a chance to correct mistakes in their data. A black-box model can also hide unfair patterns. One hiring algorithm reportedly learned to downgrade resumes that mentioned women's organizations, and it was hard to detect because nobody understood how the system worked.

Marisol: I think a strict requirement could do more harm than good. In medicine, for example, a more accurate model could correctly identify patients at risk of serious illness whom a simpler model would miss. Choosing a less accurate model means accepting more wrong decisions, and those errors affect real people too. Instead, organizations should test complex models carefully for bias and allow people to appeal decisions.
sampleAnswer: This trade-off is challenging, but I agree with Lars that explainability should be required for high-stakes decisions about people. Marisol makes a fair point about medicine, yet the accuracy gap is often smaller than people assume. Researchers have found that for many structured datasets, like loan applications or patient records, carefully designed simple models perform almost as well as complex ones. Therefore, organizations frequently sacrifice very little accuracy by choosing interpretable models. Another reason to require explainability is that it helps organizations improve their own systems. When analysts can see which factors drive predictions, they can notice when a model relies on a meaningless or outdated pattern, such as a hospital billing code that changed years ago. With a black-box model, such errors may continue unnoticed until they cause serious harm. Finally, Marisol suggests allowing appeals, but an appeal is nearly meaningless if no one can explain the original decision. For these reasons, I support requiring interpretable models.

prompt: Dr. Fontaine: Marine protected areas, or MPAs, are regions of the ocean where human activities are restricted to conserve ecosystems. In response, some places have introduced daily visitor limits, entry fees for day-trippers, or advance reservation systems. Supporters argue these measures protect fragile sites and communities. Critics respond that they make travel more expensive and exclusive, harm small businesses that depend on tourism, and simply push crowds to nearby destinations. Should popular destinations restrict the number of visitors they allow? Explain your position, considering the interests of residents, businesses, and travelers.
passage:
Simon: Yes, I think limits are necessary. In Venice, the number of permanent residents has fallen sharply over recent decades, partly because apartments have been converted into short-term rentals and daily life has become difficult with so many crowds. If a destination loses its residents and its character, it eventually loses what attracted tourists in the first place. A limit protects the long-term value of the place.

Talia: I'm against strict caps. They would turn famous places into luxury experiences for people who can afford to book months in advance and pay high fees. Students and lower-income travelers would be excluded. Instead, cities could spread visitors out by promoting lesser-known neighborhoods, encouraging travel in the off-season, and limiting cruise ships, which bring huge crowds for only a few hours.
sampleAnswer: I agree with Simon that popular destinations should be allowed to restrict visitor numbers, although Talia raises a valid concern about fairness. To address it, destinations could reserve a portion of daily entry spots for low-cost tickets distributed by lottery, so access is not determined only by money. My main reason for supporting limits is that some sites face physical damage that cannot be undone. At Machu Picchu, for example, thousands of footsteps every day gradually wear down ancient stone paths and terraces. Promoting other neighborhoods, as Talia suggests, may relieve crowded city streets, but it cannot help a single irreplaceable archaeological site that everyone wants to see. Furthermore, limits can actually improve visitors' experiences. Anyone who has struggled to see a famous painting over a crowd of raised phones knows that overcrowding makes a visit less meaningful. For these reasons, I believe carefully designed visitor limits benefit residents, sites, and tourists alike.

prompt: Dr. Iqbal: Sports equipment has changed dramatically thanks to advances in materials science. Some argue that technological progress is a natural part of sport, just like better training and nutrition. Others believe that when equipment provides a large advantage, competitions measure technology rather than athletic ability, and athletes without access to the latest products are left behind. Should sports governing bodies strictly limit performance-enhancing equipment? Explain your view.
passage:
Malik: I think strict limits are necessary. Sports are supposed to compare athletes, not engineering departments. When the high-tech swimsuits were allowed, long-standing records fell almost every week, and some of those records became almost impossible to break once the suits were banned. Athletes from smaller countries or with smaller sponsorship deals also couldn't access the newest equipment, which made competition unfair.

Selin: I believe some technological progress should be accepted. Pole vaulters once used bamboo poles and later switched to fiberglass, and no one today thinks modern vaulters are cheating. New equipment can also reduce injuries; well-cushioned shoes help protect runners' joints. As long as the equipment is available to all athletes at a reasonable price, it shouldn't be banned simply because it improves performance.
sampleAnswer: I agree with Selin that technological progress should generally be accepted in sports, although Malik's concern about unequal access is important. The key, as Selin suggests, is to require that any approved equipment be commercially available to every competitor well before major events, which several governing bodies have started doing. A point that neither classmate mentioned is that strict limits would be extremely difficult to define and enforce. Nearly every piece of modern equipment, from tennis rackets to bicycles, involves advanced materials, so officials would have to decide exactly where improvement becomes unacceptable. This creates endless disputes and might block beneficial innovations, such as safer helmets or better prosthetic limbs for para-athletes. Moreover, the history of sport shows that new equipment often makes events more exciting for fans and encourages more people to participate. Instead of strict bans, governing bodies should set clear standards for fairness and availability. For these reasons, I believe innovation should be regulated thoughtfully rather than heavily restricted.

prompt: Dr. Okafor: In our unit on ethnographic methods, we discussed how anthropologists gain insight into a culture by spending long periods in a single community. Many students also want to experience other cultures directly, for example during a summer or semester abroad. Some people argue that the best way to understand a foreign culture is to stay in one place, such as living with a host family for several months. Others believe it is better to travel widely across a country, visiting many cities and regions to see how much variety exists. If your goal were to understand another culture, which approach would you choose: living with one host family or traveling to many places? Explain why.
passage:
Hana: I would choose living with a host family. When you stay in one home, you see ordinary routines that tourists never notice, like how meals are shared, how decisions are made, and how people treat older relatives. My cousin lived with a family in Peru for four months, and she said the most important lessons came from small daily conversations, not from famous sights. Depth matters more than variety.

Marco: I think traveling widely is the better choice. A single family can give you a very narrow picture, because every household is different. If you only stay in one village, you might assume that everyone in the country thinks the same way. By visiting cities, rural areas, and different regions, you can compare dialects, food, and attitudes, and you understand the culture as a whole rather than one small part of it.
sampleAnswer: I side with Hana, although Marco is right that one household cannot represent an entire country. In my view, the real barrier to understanding another culture is not a lack of variety but a lack of trust. Travelers are treated as guests, so people show them a polite, carefully prepared version of their lives. A host family, by contrast, eventually stops performing. After a few weeks, you start to hear honest opinions, notice disagreements, and learn the unwritten rules that guide behavior. Language is another important factor. Living with a family forces you to use the local language every day, and language carries cultural ideas that cannot easily be translated. For example, a friend who stayed with a family in Japan only understood the importance of indirect refusals after she accidentally offended her host mother. Marco's concern could be solved with a few short trips at the end of the stay, but the depth of a home stay is difficult to replace.

prompt: Dr. Novak: We have been studying second language acquisition, including research suggesting that young children are especially good at picking up the sounds of a new language. However, other studies show that older learners often make faster progress at first, because they can understand grammar rules and use effective study strategies. passage:
Yuki: I believe schools should start in first grade. Young children are not afraid of making mistakes, so they happily repeat new words and sounds. That relaxed attitude is hard to recover later. In my elementary school, we had Spanish twice a week starting at age six, and many of my classmates still have a much better accent than people who started in high school. Early exposure also makes a new language seem like a normal part of life.

Daniel: I think it is better to wait until middle school. First graders still need to build strong reading and math skills in their first language, and adding another subject may take time away from those basics. Older students can learn more in a shorter time because they already understand how grammar works.
sampleAnswer: Although I appreciate Daniel's concern about limited class time, I agree with Yuki that schools should begin foreign language instruction in first grade. A student who begins at six has seven or eight years of experience by the time he or she enters high school. Another benefit that has not been mentioned is that early language study can improve children's understanding of their own language. When my younger sister learned basic French, she began asking why English puts adjectives before nouns, which showed she was thinking about grammar in a new way. As for the shortage of teachers, schools could combine video lessons by native speakers with simple classroom activities. In my opinion, the long-term benefits clearly outweigh the costs.

prompt: Dr. Hartmann: This week we compared two classic views of the good life. Hedonists argue that a good life is one with as much pleasure and as little pain as possible. Other philosophers, including Aristotle, suggest that a good life comes from developing our abilities and pursuing worthwhile goals, even when this involves difficulty and struggle. Modern psychology has added evidence to both sides of this debate. For this discussion, think about your own experience and observations. Which contributes more to a good life: seeking comfort and enjoyable experiences, or pursuing challenging goals that require effort and sacrifice? Explain your reasoning.
passage:
Leila: I think pursuing challenging goals contributes more to a good life. Comfort feels nice, but it fades quickly, and people often become bored. When I trained for a half marathon last year, many days were painful, but finishing the race gave me a sense of pride that still motivates me today. Struggle gives our lives a story and a direction, which simple pleasure cannot provide.

Omar: In my view, people underestimate the value of comfort and enjoyment. Many people chase difficult goals because society tells them to, and they end up stressed and exhausted. My uncle worked extremely long hours to become a manager, and he later said he regretted missing time with his children. Simple pleasures like good meals, hobbies, and relaxing with friends are what people remember most at the end of their lives.
sampleAnswer: I agree with Leila that challenging goals contribute more to a good life, though Omar's story about his uncle is a useful warning. I think the problem in that example was not the challenge itself but choosing the wrong goal. My main reason is that pleasure tends to lose its effect when we repeat it. The first week of a vacation feels wonderful, but by the third week many people feel restless. Challenges, on the other hand, keep producing satisfaction because they help us grow. When I started learning the piano at nineteen, I was frustrated for months, yet every small improvement gave me a deeper kind of happiness than watching another television series. Furthermore, challenging goals often bring people together, since we usually need teammates, teachers, or friends to achieve them. In that sense, a life of meaningful effort can include many of the relationships that Omar values.

Sofia: I think museums should allow photography. When people post pictures of paintings on social media, their friends become curious and may visit the museum themselves. prompt: Dr. Castillo: In our music education unit, we have looked at different methods for teaching beginners. Traditional programs usually start by teaching students to read musical notation, so they can play written pieces accurately. Other approaches, such as the Suzuki method, emphasize learning by ear first. Should they learn to read notation first, or should they begin by learning to play by ear? Explain why.
passage:
Ines: I think learning by ear should come first. Music is about sound, not symbols on a page. When I started guitar, I learned songs by listening to recordings, and it trained me to hear rhythm and pitch carefully. Students who begin with notation often become dependent on the page and cannot play anything without it. Learning by ear also makes lessons more fun, so beginners are less likely to quit.

Tomas: I believe beginners should learn to read notation from the start. Reading music is like reading a language: it opens up thousands of pieces that you could never learn just by listening. My piano teacher taught me notation in the first month, and by the end of the year I could play simple classical pieces I had never heard before. Learning to read later is much harder because students resist it.
sampleAnswer: Although Tomas makes a strong point about access to written music, I agree with Ines that beginners should learn by ear first. The main reason is motivation. The biggest problem in music education is not slow progress but students quitting in the first year, and reading notation can feel like doing math homework before you are allowed to make music. When beginners can play a familiar melody within a few lessons, they feel successful and want to continue. Another benefit that has not been mentioned is that ear training helps students play with other people. In my school band, the students who had learned by ear were much better at adjusting when someone played out of tune, while others just kept following the page. Of course, students should eventually learn notation, as Tomas suggests. However, it will be easier and more meaningful once they already understand how music sounds and feels.

prompt: Dr. Patel: In journalism, there has always been tension between being first and being right. Should your outlet publish quickly with the information available, or wait until every detail is verified? Explain your position.
passage:
Amara: I think the outlet should wait until the details are verified. Readers trust a local news site precisely because it is careful. The correction came later, but the damage was already done.

Lucas: I believe the outlet should publish quickly but clearly label what is unconfirmed. If a local site stays silent, people will simply get their information from rumors on social media, which are often far less accurate. sampleAnswer: I agree with Lucas that a local outlet should publish quickly, as long as it is honest about what it does not know. For instance, during a flood in my hometown, the local newspaper posted short verified updates every hour, and people relied on it instead of panicking over viral videos. Publishing quickly also allows readers to send in tips and photos that help journalists confirm the story faster. Therefore, I think careful, transparent speed serves the public better than complete silence.

Requiring mediation first would free up the courts for problems that truly need a legal ruling. In my math class, our teacher allowed retakes, and I studied the topics I had failed much more carefully the second time. I actually learned the material.

That said, Andre's point about distracting noises is valid. prompt: Dr. Mensah: Our readings this week examined the history of museum collections, many of which include objects acquired from other societies during periods of colonial rule or unequal trade. Today, some communities are asking museums to return these artifacts. Supporters of repatriation argue that the objects are part of living cultural traditions and belong with the people who created them. Others contend that major museums can preserve fragile objects more effectively and allow millions of international visitors to learn about world cultures. Weighing these considerations, should museums return cultural artifacts to their communities of origin, or should such objects remain in major international museums? Defend your position.
passage:
Kwame: I believe museums should generally return these artifacts. For many communities, a ceremonial mask or carved post is not merely an object to be admired behind glass; it is part of ongoing religious or social practices. Keeping it in a distant museum disconnects it from its meaning. Moreover, returning objects can rebuild trust, and many communities now have their own museums capable of caring for them properly.

Isabel: I see the moral argument, but I think a blanket policy of return could be harmful. Some objects are extremely fragile and require specialized climate control that not every institution can provide. Also, large museums let visitors compare cultures side by side, which promotes understanding. A better compromise might be long-term loans, shared ownership, or digital replicas, allowing communities access while keeping the objects safe and widely visible.
sampleAnswer: Isabel's concern about preservation is reasonable, but I side with Kwame that museums should, in most cases, return cultural artifacts. The preservation argument assumes that only wealthy museums can protect important objects, yet museums could transfer not just the artifacts but also funding and expertise. Several European institutions have already helped partner countries build conservation laboratories. More fundamentally, I think the value of an object depends on who can interpret it. The meaning of a ritual object often lives in songs, stories, and ceremonies that only its original community preserves. When a drum is displayed silently in a foreign gallery, visitors see its shape but miss its purpose. Isabel's idea of shared ownership is appealing, but it still leaves the final decision with the institution that acquired the object under unequal conditions. Returning artifacts, combined with traveling exhibitions organized by the communities themselves, could actually give international audiences a richer understanding than permanent displays do.

prompt: Dr. Ivanova: Linguists estimate that nearly half of the world's roughly seven thousand languages may disappear by the end of this century, as younger generations shift to more widely spoken languages. Should governments invest significant public funds in preserving endangered languages? Explain your reasoning.

Ayasha: I believe governments should invest in preservation. When a language disappears, we lose knowledge about local plants, history, and ways of thinking that are often impossible to translate. Moreover, many language shifts happened because of past policies that discouraged minority languages in schools, so governments bear some responsibility for repairing that damage. Funding immersion programs gives communities a genuine choice rather than pressuring them to abandon their heritage.

Lars: I sympathize with preservation efforts, but I question whether large government programs are the right tool. Many young people switch languages because the dominant language offers better jobs and education, and funding cannot change that reality. Money spent on revitalization might help more if used for job training or schools. Recording and documenting endangered languages is reasonable, but communities, not governments, should lead efforts to keep them alive.
sampleAnswer: Lars raises a practical point about economic incentives, but I agree with Ayasha that governments should invest substantially in endangered languages. Lars presents the choice as language versus economic opportunity, yet research on bilingual education suggests these goals are not in conflict. Children who learn their heritage language alongside the national language often perform as well academically as other students, and sometimes better, because they develop a stronger awareness of how language works. Furthermore, there is evidence that revitalization benefits community well-being. Studies of Indigenous communities in Canada, for instance, have linked stronger language knowledge to better mental health among young people, possibly because language reinforces identity and connections between generations. If that is true, language funding is also a public health investment. I do agree with Lars that communities should lead these programs, since top-down projects rarely succeed. However, community leadership and government funding can work together: the state provides resources, while local speakers design curricula that reflect their own priorities.

prompt: Dr. Lindgren: In recent lectures, we compared two major traditions in ethics. Consequentialists argue that an action is right or wrong depending on its results: what matters is whether it produces more good than harm. Other philosophers, influenced by Kant, emphasize the agent's intentions and principles, holding that a person who acts from good will deserves moral credit even if things turn out badly. Consider someone who donates to a charity that later proves to be badly managed, or someone who acts selfishly but accidentally helps others. When judging whether an action was morally good, should we focus primarily on intentions or on consequences? Explain.
passage:
Noor: I think intentions should matter more. People cannot control or predict every outcome, so judging them by consequences seems unfair. A person who donates to a charity in good faith has done everything morally required of them; the charity's poor management is not their fault. If we focused only on results, we would be praising people for lucky accidents, which makes morality seem random rather than a matter of character.

Henrik: I lean toward consequences, though not completely. Good intentions are cheap if people make no effort to understand the effects of their actions. Someone who donates without researching the charity has, in a way, been careless. In areas like medicine or public policy, we judge decisions by their outcomes because real people are affected. Intentions matter, but they should not excuse a failure to think ahead.
sampleAnswer: I find myself agreeing with Henrik that consequences deserve more weight, though Noor's point about luck is important. I think the solution is to judge people by the consequences they could reasonably foresee. This approach avoids praising lucky accidents, which concerns Noor, while still holding people responsible for considering the effects of their choices. My additional reason is that a focus on intentions is easily manipulated. Almost everyone believes their own intentions are good, including people who cause serious harm. A company that pollutes a river might sincerely believe it is creating jobs for the community, but that belief does not reduce the damage to families living downstream. If moral judgment depends mainly on what happens inside someone's mind, it becomes almost impossible to criticize anyone. Consequences, by contrast, can be observed and debated publicly. Therefore, while intentions reveal something about a person's character, I believe the rightness of an action should be judged mainly by its foreseeable results.

prompt: Dr. Rossi: This week we examined several famous restoration projects, including the cleaning of the Sistine Chapel ceiling in the 1980s and 1990s, which revealed surprisingly bright colors beneath centuries of grime. Some critics praised the result, while others claimed restorers had removed final touches the artist himself had added. Restorers today face a difficult choice. One approach aims to return an artwork as closely as possible to its original appearance. Another focuses on stabilizing the work and preventing further damage while preserving signs of age and history. Which approach should guide the treatment of damaged artworks: restoring their original appearance or conserving them in their current condition? Defend your view.
passage:
Camille: I think conservation should be the guiding principle. Every intervention risks destroying information we cannot recover, and our knowledge of an artist's original intentions is always incomplete. The aging of a painting is also part of its history; cracks and faded colors show that it has survived for centuries. Future generations may have better technology, so we should do the minimum necessary and leave major decisions to them.

Raj: I would argue for careful restoration. Many artworks were meant to be seen in bright, vivid colors, and dirt or yellowed varnish completely changes their effect. Viewers who see a darkened painting misunderstand the artist's style, which is why some Renaissance painters were once thought to prefer dull tones. As long as restorers document their work and use reversible materials, restoration brings us closer to the artist's vision.
sampleAnswer: Raj makes a persuasive case, particularly with his point about reversible materials, but I agree with Camille that conservation should guide the treatment of damaged artworks. The central problem is that restoration depends on assumptions about what the original looked like, and those assumptions reflect the taste of each era. In the nineteenth century, for example, some restorers repainted older works to fit fashionable ideas of beauty, and later experts spent decades undoing those changes. There is no reason to believe our generation is immune to the same bias. Another consideration is that an artwork's 'original appearance' is not always a single moment. Many artists revised their works over years, and some objects were intentionally altered by later owners for religious or practical reasons. Choosing one version erases the others. That said, I accept Raj's view that heavy dirt can seriously distort a work, so removing surface grime is reasonable. Beyond that, though, restorers should stabilize rather than reinvent.

prompt: Dr. Whitaker: In our literary theory unit, we encountered the debate over whether an author's life and intentions should shape how we interpret a work. Biographical critics study letters, diaries, and historical context to understand what writers meant. In contrast, critics like Roland Barthes famously declared 'the death of the author,' arguing that once a text is published, its meaning is created by readers, and the author's intentions have no special authority. When interpreting a novel or poem, should readers give significant weight to the author's biography and stated intentions, or should the text be interpreted on its own terms? Explain your view.

Thandiwe: I believe the author's life and context matter significantly. Literature is created by real people in specific historical moments, and ignoring that can lead to serious misreadings. For example, knowing that a novelist wrote under wartime censorship helps us notice hidden criticism that would otherwise seem like simple description. Without context, readers may impose modern assumptions that the author could never have imagined.

Gabriel: I lean toward interpreting the text on its own terms. Authors often do not fully understand their own works, and their statements about them can be misleading or change over time. Some of the most interesting readings of classic novels come from perspectives the authors never considered. Besides, for many older texts, we know almost nothing about the author's life, yet we still read them meaningfully.
sampleAnswer: Both classmates make valid points, but I am more persuaded by Gabriel that the text should remain the primary authority. Thandiwe's example of wartime censorship is useful, though I would note that historical context is not the same as an author's personal intentions. We can study the conditions of a period without assuming we know what a particular writer meant. My main reason is that relying heavily on biography can narrow a work's meaning instead of enriching it. When readers learn that a poet suffered personal tragedies, they sometimes reduce every dark image to autobiography, ignoring the poem's craft, humor, or ambiguity. Sylvia Plath's poetry, for instance, has often been read almost entirely through her life story, which many critics believe has overshadowed her technical skill. In addition, great literature survives precisely because new generations find fresh meanings in it. If interpretation were limited to the author's intentions, those works would become historical documents rather than living art.

prompt: Dr. Calloway: Anonymous sources have played a crucial role in some of the most important investigative stories in history, allowing whistleblowers to reveal wrongdoing without risking their jobs or safety. Malik: I think anonymous sources remain essential. Many government and corporate abuses would never have been exposed if insiders had been forced to reveal their names. Anna: While I recognize their value in investigative reporting, I think anonymous sources are now overused. sampleAnswer: I agree with Anna that anonymous sources should be strictly limited, although Malik is right that whistleblowers must be protected. If unnamed sources appear in every article, readers cannot distinguish a brave insider revealing fraud from an official spreading convenient rumors. Governments and companies sometimes leak information anonymously to test public reaction to a plan or to damage competitors, knowing they will never be held responsible. When journalists grant anonymity too easily, they risk becoming tools of the people they should be investigating. A practical solution would be for news organizations to publish a brief explanation whenever they use an anonymous source, describing why the person needed protection and how the information was verified. prompt: Dr. Nakamura: Laws and legal contracts are notoriously difficult for ordinary people to understand. Long sentences, technical terms, and Latin phrases often mean that citizens must hire lawyers simply to know their rights. In response, a plain-language movement has encouraged governments to rewrite statutes and official documents in clear, everyday language. Critics caution, however, that legal terminology exists for a reason: established terms have precise meanings developed through decades of court decisions, and simplifying them could create ambiguity and new disputes. Should governments rewrite laws in plain language that ordinary people can understand, even if some precision might be lost? Explain your reasoning.
passage:
Selin: I strongly support plain-language laws. In a democracy, people are expected to obey the law, so they should be able to read and understand it. Currently, lower-income citizens are at a disadvantage because they cannot afford lawyers to explain their rental agreements or employment rights. Clear writing would make the legal system fairer. Several countries have successfully simplified tax forms without major problems.

Patrick: I agree that legal language is often too complex, but I worry about rewriting existing laws. Terms like 'reasonable care' have meanings defined by hundreds of court cases. If legislators replace them with everyday words, judges would have to interpret the new language from scratch, causing years of uncertainty and more lawsuits. A safer approach would be to provide official plain-language summaries alongside the original legal text.
sampleAnswer: Selin's argument about fairness is compelling, but I find Patrick's proposal more realistic, since rewriting existing laws could create exactly the confusion that plain language is meant to prevent. However, I would go further than Patrick in one respect: new laws, unlike old ones, should be written in plain language from the beginning. Because they have no history of court interpretation yet, there is no established precision to lose. Over time, the legal system would gradually become more accessible without disrupting settled areas of law. Another reason for caution is that simplicity can be misleading. A sentence that seems clear to an ordinary reader may hide important exceptions, and people might feel confident about their rights when they are actually mistaken. For instance, a simplified lease stating that tenants 'may end the contract early' could omit the conditions and penalties involved. Official summaries, clearly labeled as guides rather than binding text, would help citizens grasp the general picture while still encouraging them to seek advice in complex situations.

These techniques can significantly increase sales. However, critics argue that they pressure consumers into hasty decisions, and when customers discover that the scarcity was exaggerated, they may lose trust in the brand. In your view, are scarcity tactics a legitimate marketing tool, or do their long-term costs to customer trust outweigh their short-term benefits? Explain your position.
passage:
Freya: I think scarcity tactics are legitimate when they are honest. Limited-edition products, such as seasonal flavors or collaborations with artists, create excitement and give customers something to look forward to. As long as the stock levels and deadlines are real, the company is simply sharing accurate information. Customers are adults who can decide for themselves whether they truly want something.

Hassan: In my opinion, these tactics usually do more harm than good. Many countdown timers simply restart when you refresh the page, which is plainly deceptive. Even when scarcity is real, the pressure encourages impulse purchases that customers later regret, leading to more returns and negative reviews. Brands that build long-term relationships rely on quality and trust, not artificial urgency that makes shoppers feel manipulated.
sampleAnswer: I share Hassan's concern about deceptive timers, but I agree with Freya that scarcity tactics can be legitimate, as long as they reflect reality. The key distinction, in my view, is between scarcity that is built into the product and scarcity that is invented by the website. A limited run of handmade sneakers or a concert with a fixed number of seats is genuinely scarce, and telling customers so is useful information. A fake 'only two left' message, on the other hand, is simply a lie. One point that has not been raised is that honest scarcity can benefit consumers and the environment. When companies produce limited quantities based on real demand, they create less unsold inventory, which often ends up heavily discounted or thrown away. Some fashion brands have reduced waste by releasing small collections instead of mass-producing every design. Therefore, rather than rejecting scarcity marketing entirely, regulators and companies should focus on banning misleading claims while allowing truthful limited releases.

prompt: Dr. Ashworth: When a senior leadership position opens, organizations face a familiar dilemma: should they promote someone from within or recruit an outside candidate? Internal candidates already understand the company's culture and processes, and promoting them can motivate other employees. External candidates, however, may bring new ideas, skills, and a willingness to challenge established practices, which can be crucial when an organization needs to change. Research shows mixed results, with outcomes depending heavily on circumstances. Imagine a mid-sized company whose sales have been declining for two years. Should it fill its vacant CEO position with an internal candidate or an external hire? Justify your recommendation.
passage:
Ingrid: I would recommend an internal candidate. Someone who has worked at the company for years understands its customers, products, and employees, so he or she can act quickly instead of spending months learning. Bringing in an outsider during a crisis can also damage morale, because employees may feel their loyalty is not valued. Studies have found that external CEOs are often paid more but do not necessarily perform better.

Carlos: Given that sales have been falling for two years, I would choose an external hire. Internal candidates were part of the leadership that allowed the decline, and they may be too attached to existing strategies to make difficult changes. An outsider can see problems more objectively and is not tied to internal friendships or office politics. Sometimes a company needs a fresh perspective more than familiarity.
sampleAnswer: Ingrid makes a fair point about morale, but in this specific situation I agree with Carlos that the company should hire an external CEO. The fact that sales have declined for two consecutive years suggests a structural problem rather than bad luck, and structural problems usually require questioning assumptions that insiders take for granted. An internal candidate may also feel obligated to protect colleagues or projects he or she helped create. One argument that has not been mentioned is the signal an external hire sends to investors, suppliers, and customers. Announcing a leader with a strong record of turning companies around can rebuild confidence and attract the funding a struggling firm may need. IBM's recovery in the 1990s under Lou Gerstner, who came from outside the computer industry, is a well-known example. Nevertheless, Ingrid's concern deserves attention. To protect morale, the new CEO should promote talented internal managers into key roles, combining a fresh perspective with deep institutional knowledge.

prompt: Dr. Kaplan: One of the most consequential decisions founders make is how to finance their startup. Some seek venture capital, accepting large investments in exchange for a share of ownership and, often, pressure to grow quickly. Others choose bootstrapping, funding the business through personal savings and revenue, which allows them to keep full control but usually means slower growth. Both paths have produced successful companies, and both have led to failures. Imagine a founder who has developed a promising app for managing small restaurants' inventories. Should she pursue venture capital funding or bootstrap the company? Explain the trade-offs that inform your recommendation.
passage:
Zara: I would recommend venture capital. The software market moves quickly, and if this app is successful, competitors will copy it. Investment money would allow the founder to hire developers and salespeople and capture the market before others do. Experienced investors also offer valuable advice and connections, such as introductions to large restaurant chains, which a bootstrapped founder would struggle to obtain alone.

Ivan: I would advise bootstrapping. Restaurants operate on thin margins and are cautious about new technology, so this market may grow slowly no matter how much money is invested. Venture capitalists often expect rapid expansion, which could push the founder to spend heavily before the product is ready. By growing gradually with paying customers, she can keep control and build a sustainable business rather than chase unrealistic growth targets.
sampleAnswer: Zara's concern about competitors is understandable, but I agree with Ivan that the founder should bootstrap, at least at first. Ivan's observation about restaurants' thin margins is especially relevant: in a market that adopts technology slowly, extra money cannot easily speed up customer decisions, and spending heavily on salespeople might produce little more than expensive rejections. I would add that bootstrapping forces the founder to listen carefully to her customers. When revenue is the only source of funding, every feature must solve a real problem that restaurant owners are willing to pay for. Mailchimp, for example, grew for nearly two decades without outside investment, and this discipline kept the company focused on customer needs. Moreover, once the founder has proven that restaurants value the app, she will be in a much stronger position to negotiate with investors if she later decides to accept funding, giving up a smaller share of the company for the same amount of money. In short, patience now could provide more options later.

prompt: Dr. Mwangi: Ability grouping, or tracking, places students into separate classes based on their current academic performance. Supporters argue that it allows teachers to adjust the pace of instruction, challenging advanced students while giving struggling students more support. Critics point to research suggesting that students placed in lower tracks often receive less demanding instruction, lose motivation, and rarely move to higher groups, which can widen achievement gaps. Mixed-ability classrooms avoid these problems but may make it difficult for teachers to meet everyone's needs. Should secondary schools group students by ability, or should they maintain mixed-ability classes? Discuss the competing considerations and explain your position.
passage:
Sakura: I believe ability grouping is more effective. In my mixed-ability math class, the teacher had to explain basic concepts repeatedly, and the stronger students became bored and stopped paying attention. Meanwhile, students who were struggling felt embarrassed to ask questions in front of classmates who understood everything immediately. Separate groups allow each student to learn at an appropriate pace and feel comfortable participating.

Kofi: Although tracking sounds efficient, I think mixed-ability classes are fairer. Placement decisions are often made early and based on a single test, so a student who had a difficult year may be stuck in a lower track permanently. Moreover, students learn a great deal from explaining ideas to one another. In my experience, helping classmates deepened my own understanding, and they benefited from hearing explanations in student-friendly language.
sampleAnswer: I agree with Kofi that secondary schools should generally keep mixed-ability classes, although Sakura's experience shows that they must be well managed. The problem she describes, a teacher repeating basic explanations for the whole class, results from a teaching method rather than the class composition. Teachers can divide a mixed class into small groups for certain activities, giving advanced students more challenging tasks while providing extra support to others, all within the same room. My main concern about tracking is its effect on expectations. When students are labeled as 'low ability' at the age of twelve, both teachers and students tend to lower their goals, and those expectations often become self-fulfilling. A cousin of mine was placed in a lower track after moving schools and missing a placement exam, and it took him three years to convince the school he belonged in an advanced class. In addition, mixed classes prepare students for workplaces where they will collaborate with people of different backgrounds and skill levels.

prompt: Dr. Holloway: In social psychology, research on group decision-making has produced seemingly contradictory findings. On one hand, the 'wisdom of crowds' suggests that combining many people's judgments often produces more accurate estimates than any individual expert. On the other hand, studies of groupthink show that cohesive groups sometimes make disastrous choices because members suppress doubts in order to maintain harmony. Organizations, juries, and governments must regularly decide how much to rely on collective deliberation versus individual judgment. In your view, do groups generally make better decisions than individuals, or do the risks of group dynamics outweigh the benefits? Support your position with reasons or examples.
passage:
Valentina: I believe groups generally make better decisions. Each person has blind spots, and a group can compensate for them by bringing together different knowledge and perspectives. In my economics project, I was confident about a forecast until a teammate pointed out a mistake in my assumptions. Groups also share responsibility, which makes members more careful. Groupthink is a real risk, but it can be prevented with good procedures.

Jamal: I think the risks of group dynamics are often underestimated. In many groups, the most confident or senior person dominates the discussion, and others simply agree to avoid conflict. Then the group's decision is really one person's opinion with false confidence attached. Groups also take much longer to decide. For urgent decisions, a single well-informed person who is accountable for the outcome is often more effective.
sampleAnswer: Jamal describes a common problem, but I agree with Valentina that groups generally make better decisions, as long as they are structured correctly. The key insight from 'wisdom of crowds' research is that groups perform well only when members form their opinions independently before influencing one another. The failures Jamal mentions usually happen when people discuss first and think later, so the most confident voice shapes everyone's judgment. A simple remedy is to have members write down their views privately before any discussion begins. Some companies, including Amazon, reportedly open meetings by having everyone silently read a written proposal and form their own conclusions, which reduces the influence of senior employees. Another benefit of group decisions that has not been mentioned is legitimacy. When people participate in a decision, they are more likely to accept and implement it, even if they initially disagreed. A brilliant individual decision that nobody supports may fail in practice. Thus, well-designed groups combine accuracy with commitment in a way individuals cannot.

prompt: Dr. Duval: Adaptation has been central to cinema since its earliest days, and many of the most celebrated films are based on novels. Yet audiences frequently complain when a film changes the plot, removes beloved characters, or alters the ending of a book they love. Some filmmakers argue that film and literature are fundamentally different media, so a faithful copy often produces a weaker movie; a successful adaptation must reinterpret its source. Others believe filmmakers have an obligation to respect the original author's work and the readers who cherish it. Should film adaptations remain faithful to their source material, or should directors take significant creative liberties? Explain your position.
passage:
Lucia: I believe adaptations should remain largely faithful. When filmmakers use a famous title, they benefit from the book's reputation and its loyal readers, so they have a responsibility to respect the story. Changing major events or characters can feel like a betrayal. The Harry Potter films succeeded partly because they stayed close to the books, and fans appreciated seeing scenes they had imagined brought to life.

Arjun: I think directors should feel free to take creative liberties. Novels can spend pages describing a character's thoughts, but film must communicate through images, sound, and action. A strictly faithful adaptation is often slow and confusing. Some of the greatest adaptations, such as The Godfather, cut entire subplots and arguably improved the story. A film should be judged as a film, not as a copy of a book.
sampleAnswer: Lucia's point about the responsibilities that come with a famous title is reasonable, but I agree with Arjun that directors should be allowed significant creative liberties. Faithfulness to the plot does not guarantee faithfulness to the spirit of a book, and the spirit is what truly matters. For example, Stanley Kubrick's version of The Shining changed many details from Stephen King's novel, and King himself disliked it, yet critics widely consider it one of the most powerful horror films ever made. Kubrick used visual techniques, such as long tracking shots through empty hallways, to create a sense of isolation that no scene-by-scene copy could have achieved. An additional reason is that a creative adaptation can actually benefit the original book. When a film offers a different interpretation, it often encourages viewers to read the novel and compare the two versions, which keeps the book in public conversation. A faithful but forgettable film, by contrast, adds little to either the novel or the art of cinema.
